texts: We normally use simple present tense to talk about countries and nationalities. Not only the verb to be can be useful to talk about this. Revise the following chart and check some examples.
Even when we talk about this topic, the grammar rules must be respected.
The verb to be is an independent verb it can say a sentence, it can make a question or deny by itself. NO AUXILIARY NEEDED

The rest of the verbs are dependent. They use auxiliaries to make questions and to deny an action. 

Do - I/You/We/They
Does - He/She/ It (3rd person singular)
*Pronunciation hint: https://youtu.be/EMWmCb1CIdc

texts: It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about routines; also, the use of adverbs of frequency is common on this topic.
They normally go to the beach on Saturdays
Carol hardly ever takes a call.
1. Adverbs go before verbs since they modify them, EXCEPT for To Be.
3. Adverbs can work in statements, negative sentences and questions.
slides.joinedText:
It is common to use the simple present tense to talk about routines; also, the use of adverbs of frequency is common on this topic.
ADVERBS OF FREQUENCY
100%
Always
We always work at night.
90%
Usually
She is usually late.
80%
Normally
They normally go to the beach on Saturdays
70%
Often
I am often at home.
50%
Sometimes
You sometimes laugh out loud.
30%
Occasionally
He occasionally cleans his room.
10%
Seldom
It seldom rains here.
5%
Hardly ever
Carol hardly ever takes a call.
0%
Never
John is never on time.
HINT

1. Adverbs go before verbs since they modify them, EXCEPT for To Be.
She is always happy

2. NEVER has a negative connotation. 
(no need for don’t/doesn’t)
They never visit me.

3. Adverbs can work in statements, negative sentences and questions.

texts: Talk about general actions everybody makes.
Talk about specific actions each one does.
Ruth changes Peter’s clothes  twice a day.
Talk about activities with specific time of occurrence.
Ruth has English class at 6 pm
When we talk about daily routines there are three main aspects that we should take into account using the simple present tense.

The three aspects talk about the same function but they aim different targets in language. The second aspect, as seen in the example, uses mainly general or indefinite time expressions to differentiate itself from the third one.

texts: It is common to use verbs that state preferences when we talk about hobbies. Check the following chart.
I am fond of playing soccer.
NOT TO BE A FAN OF
I am not a fan of watching horror movies.
I am thrilled about reading books.
Notice that after a preference expression, the action can go in ing form.
slides.joinedText:
It is common to use verbs that state preferences when we talk about hobbies. Check the following chart.
MOST COMMON VERBS FOR PREFERENCES
NEGATIVE COUNTERPARTS
EXAMPLES
LIKE
DISLIKE / DON’T LIKE
She likes eating ice cream.
ENJOY
DON’T ENJOY
I don’t enjoy cooking.
LOVE
HATE
I love listening to music.
TO BE FOR PREFERENCES
NEGATIVE COUNTERPARTS
EXAMPLES
TO BE FOND OF
NOT TO BE FOND OF
I am fond of playing soccer.
TO BE A FAN OF
NOT TO BE A FAN OF
I am not a fan of watching horror movies.
TO BE THRILLED ABOUT
NOT TO BE THRILLED ABOUT
I am thrilled about reading books.
HINT

Notice that after a preference expression, the action can go in ing form.

texts: She is thrilled about learning languages.
They are fans of running marathons.
It is fond of hiding bones in the backyard.
We mainly use simple present to express likes and preferences, but there is an interesting fact we need to consider: likeness degrees.
We can also use like and preference expressions to talk about people, food, etc. (Not only for hobbies)
The expression thrilled about sometimes is substituted by crazy about.

LOW LEVEL

It is fond of hiding bones in the backyard.
We mainly use simple present to express likes and preferences, but there is an interesting fact we need to consider: likeness degrees.
HINT

We can also use like and preference expressions to talk about people, food, etc. (Not only for hobbies)

The expression thrilled about sometimes is substituted by crazy about.

Joe is a fan of riding horses but he dislikes cooking only for him. He’s crazy about camping so, he and Chester go camping twice a month.
1.   Joe likes taking care of animals.					(T)     (F)
2.  Joe doesn’t have a dog called Archie.			(T)     (F)
3.  Joe enjoys spending time with Chester.			(T)     (F)
4.  They like going swimming on Sundays.			(T)     (F)
5.  Joe is a fan of riding horses.					(T)     (F)
6.  He likes cooking only for him.					(T)     (F)
8.  Joe and Chester go camping once a month.		(T)     (F)

texts: To talk about relationships among family members, we normally use the possessive case (‘s) which denotes belonging and possession and in this case states family relationships.
There is more than one scenario for the possessive case:
a. Joe’s wife is a doctor. - One owner and one possession.
b. Those are my aunt’s (kids). -  When the noun was already mentioned and we do not need to state again.
c. This is Ted and Mary’s child. - Two owners - One possession.
d. These are Jake’s and Jill’s children - Two owners and two possessions.
When the noun finishes in ‘s’ we only add the (‘) and the end of the word. E.G. This is James’ child. When this happens, we add an extra syllable in spoken language that is pronounced /әz/.
This is not only used to talk about family. E.G. Adrian’s car is blue.
When we talk about objects or animals, it is common to use: The legs of the table / The tail of the cat. However, you may find examples using the (‘s).

texts: My name is Khai and I am from China. I am 26 years
old. I have a big family. My parents have six children,
three sons and three daughters. My siblings and I live
with them. I am the oldest. My sister Shinmei is the
second one. She is a science teacher at university and
she is 24 years old. Our brothers’ names are Tenkei
and Senku and our sisters’ names are Megumi and
Kumiko. My father is an only child so, we have no relatives on my father’s side. On my mother’s side, we have two uncles, three aunts and eleven cousins. See? We are a big family.

When we talk about objects or animals, it is common to use: The legs of the table / The tail of the cat. However, you may find examples using the (‘s).

texts: We normally use simple present tense to talk about food. Check out the following examples.
There is one apple on the table.
Is there one apple on the table?
There isn’t an apple on the table.
There are a lot of eggs in the basket.
Are there a lot of eggs in the basket?
There aren’t any of eggs in the basket.
I have some water in the bottle.
Do you have any water in the bottle?
I don’t have any water in the bottle.

To consider:
We use the expressions There is (singular) / there are (plural) to say something exists. 
We can use other verbs to talk about food. See example number 3. 
When we talk about food, we need to talk about quantity. We use containers and quantifiers: 
Some – Any – a lot of – Few / A few -  None – lots of – Much -  Many. 
Also, there are two main questions when we talk about quantities: 
How much – Used for uncountable nouns.  How much milk is there left?
How many – Used for countable nouns.  How many do you have?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We normally use simple present tense to talk about food. Check out the following examples.
STATEMENTS
QUESTIONS
NEGATIVE STATEMENTS
1.
There is one apple on the table.
Is there one apple on the table?
There isn’t an apple on the table.
2.
There are a lot of eggs in the basket.
Are there a lot of eggs in the basket?
There aren’t any of eggs in the basket.
3.
I have some water in the bottle.
Do you have any water in the bottle?
I don’t have any water in the bottle.
To consider:
We use the expressions There is (singular) / there are (plural) to say something exists. 
We can use other verbs to talk about food. See example number 3. 
When we talk about food, we need to talk about quantity. We use containers and quantifiers: 
Some – Any – a lot of – Few / A few -  None – lots of – Much -  Many. 
Also, there are two main questions when we talk about quantities: 
How much – Used for uncountable nouns.  How much milk is there left?
How many – Used for countable nouns.  How many do you have?

texts: - This / that (singular) These / Those (plural) are demonstratives we use to talk about possessions. This / These (close objects) – That / Those (far objects)
- Whose: wh word used to ask for possessions: Whose USB is this?
- Possessive adjectives can also be used to talk about belongings: This is my house.
- Every possessive adjective  has a possessive pronoun: My / Mine, Your / yours, His / His, Her / Hers, Its / Its, Our / Ours, Their / Theirs (used when we already know what we are talking about)
- Demonstrative pronouns can also work as adjectives. E.G That house is blue. Let’s watch the video on the platform.
We normally use simple present tense to talk about belongings. Check out the following examples.

Is that your house? / Whose house is that?
Are these your keys? / Whose keys are these?
Are those Mary’s children? / Whose Children are those?

texts: We normally use simple present tense to talk about places and where they are.
The park is on the Main Avenue.
IS the park on the Main Avenue? / Where is the park?
The park is not on the Main Avenue.
The public library is in front of the bank; so, take the train downtown.
How do I get to the public library?
I am not sure, Do you know where is it?
To get to the Caffe, go along the park.
Do you have to go across the park to get to the Caffe?
You don’t have to go between the park and local market to get to the Caffe.
The restaurant is opposite to the bakery.
The restaurant is not next to the bakery; it is opposite.
- Prepositions are used to indicate location.
- Downtown does not use any preposition: I am going downtown.
- More than 1 verb can be used to talk about directions. / Questions vary too.

texts: We normally talk about places and we include the use of adjectives to describe their characteristics. Adjectives are words we use to denote specificities about people, places or situations.
Mexico has the ancient ruins of the Mayas
Does Mexico have the ancient ruins of the Mayas?
No, it does not have the ancient ruins.
Santa Elena is a small, beautiful and hot town in the South of Venezuela.
It is not big or cold.
We live in a tiny and cozy town near the borders.
I live in a tiny and cozy  town but it is not quite.
Adjectives come before the object, place or people they describe.
They can also be after one verb:  My house is beautiful (mainly after To Be).
Adjectives do not change because of  gender. E.G: She is beautiful / The park is beautiful.
Adjectives are not pluralized. E.G: They are talls.❌ They are tall. ✅

We normally talk about places and we include the use of adjectives to describe their characteristics. Adjectives are words we use to denote specificities about people, places or situations.
Statements
Questions
Negative statements
1.
Mexico has the ancient ruins of the Mayas
Does Mexico have the ancient ruins of the Mayas?
No, it does not have the ancient ruins.
2.
Santa Elena is a small, beautiful and hot town in the South of Venezuela.
How is Santa Elena?
It is not big or cold.
3.
We live in a tiny and cozy town near the borders.
Where do you live?
I live in a tiny and cozy  town but it is not quite.
TO CONSIDER

Adjectives come before the object, place or people they describe.
They can also be after one verb:  My house is beautiful (mainly after To Be).
Adjectives do not change because of  gender. E.G: She is beautiful / The park is beautiful.
Adjectives are not pluralized. E.G: They are talls.❌ They are tall. ✅

texts: 1. Adjectives can be divided into two groups: / Short (1 or 2 syllables) / Long (2 or more syllables).
2. Short adjectives take the –er + than particles: Joe is taller than Jim.
3.Long adjectives take the more + than particles: It is more expensive here than there.
4.Short adjectives that finish in –y change to I + er: She is prettier than you.
5. There are irregular adjectives: Good – Better than / Bad – Worse than.
6. We use the particles ‘as / as’ to state similarities: Joe is as tall as Jake.
7. There are adjectives who do not receive comparison degrees; those adjective have absolute meaning: This is the final test / Those people are dead.
8. Less + Adjective + than is used to state inferiority between two nouns. E.G. Alex is less determined than his brother.
9. There are three levels of comparison: Superiority , Equality and Inferiority

texts: Adjectives are divided into two groups: / Short (1 or 2 syllables) / Long (2 or more syllables).
Short adjectives take the –est particles: Joe is the tallest in his family.
Long adjectives take the most  particle: It is the most expensive restaurant in the city.
Short adjectives that finish in –y change to I + est: She is the prettiest at school.
There are irregular adjectives: Good – Better than – The Best / Bad – Worse than – The Worst.
The superlative for less than is: The least. E.G: That is the least of my worries.
ABSOLUTE adjectives do not take superlative level

texts: Point out people among a group.
Jake is the smallest at home. / He seems to be the most interesting person in his family.
This is the biggest around here. /  Los Angeles is one of  the most expensive cities in USA.
Your bag is the best here. / Their car seems to be the most luxurious in the club.
This is the worst problem of the family. / They have now the most challenging situation of all.
Superlatives can deal with different aspects. they can also be used at any tense.
When using superlatives, you need to have always a context where the person /place /object /situation etc. stands out from.

4

texts: Ongoing actions are stated through the present progressive.  Check out the following examples.

Currently, They are rebuilding the house.
Are they currently rebuilding the house?
No, they are not currently rebuilding the house.

Questions

Are they talking on the phone right now?
They are not talking on the phone right now.

Is he practicing for the soccer finale these days?
He is not practicing for the soccer finale these days.

Currently, They are rebuilding the house.
Are they currently rebuilding the house?
No, they are not currently rebuilding the house.

Verb To Be acts as an auxiliary.

 Do/Does are not used here.

texts: Talking about the past can also have two main grammatical aspects to consider. To Be and other verbs.
Even in past, the verb to be is an independent verb it can say a sentence, it can make a question or deny by itself. NO AUXILIARY NEEDED
IT has two forms in past:
They were in the school this morning.
Were they in the school this morning?
John made a cake last night.
Did he make a cake last night?
I visited my family in Christmas.
Did you visit your family? / What did you do in Christmas?
The rest of the verbs are dependent. They use the past auxiliary DID.
DID works for all the pronouns.
Verbs go in simple form when DID is in the sentence.
Verbs in past are divided into two groups:
Irregular: They change. / They don’t Change.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Talking about the past can also have two main grammatical aspects to consider. To Be and other verbs.
TO CONSIDER

Even in past, the verb to be is an independent verb it can say a sentence, it can make a question or deny by itself. NO AUXILIARY NEEDED
IT has two forms in past: 
Was ( I/ He / She / It) 
            Were ( You / we / you/ They)
To Be verb
He was at home yesterday.
Was he at home yesterday?
They were in the school this morning.
Were they in the school this morning?
Other verbs – Auxiliary Introduction
John made a cake last night.
Did he make a cake last night?
I visited my family in Christmas.
Did you visit your family? / What did you do in Christmas?
TO CONSIDER
The rest of the verbs are dependent. They use the past auxiliary DID.
DID works for all the pronouns. 
Verbs go in simple form when DID is in the sentence. 
Verbs in past are divided into two groups: 
Regular: They follow a pattern. 
Irregular: They change. / They don’t Change.
Check out this video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XulHb3KEQPs&list=PL6c5c6_b89gr7bHe6Zf-CUUp_zEHkJaJK&index=2

texts: Talking about habits in the past leads us to use simple past tense structure; though, it is necessary to work with used to.
Used to is a fixed expression that comes before a verb in simple form.
If the sentence has the auxiliary DID, used to goes in simple form.
Other useful expressions: but not anymore / Back in my childhood / When I was a child / When I was younger etc.
Used to can be used in simple present tense to talk about customs people have. E.G. She is used to read the newspaper in the mornings.
John used to attend dancing classes all nights.
Did John use to attend dancing classes all nights?
I used to make cakes back in my school days.
Did you use to make cakes back in your school day?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Talking about habits in the past leads us to use simple past tense structure; though, it is necessary to work with used to.
TO CONSIDER
Used to is a fixed expression that comes before a verb in simple form. 
 If the sentence has the auxiliary DID, used to goes in simple form.
Other useful expressions: but not anymore / Back in my childhood / When I was a child / When I was younger etc. 
Used to can be used in simple present tense to talk about customs people have. E.G. She is used to read the newspaper in the mornings.
Used to
John used to attend dancing classes all nights.
Did John use to attend dancing classes all nights?
I used to make cakes back in my school days.
Did you use to make cakes back in your school day?

texts: When we talk about actions happening in the past, we need to use the past progressive tense.
We use the verb to be as auxiliary. In both forms: was / were.
The main verb takes the –ing form as seen in the examples.
When is used to connect two ideas; in this case it presents an action that interrupts another one.
While is used to state two actions happening simultaneously.
I was eating when the earthquake started.
Were you eating when the earthquake started?
They were relaxing at the beach when they gave the tsunami alert.
Were they relaxing at the beach when they gave the tsunami alert?
He was running fast while the tornado was chasing him.
Was he running fast while the tornado was chasing him?

texts: 2 years ago, my family and I went to Thailand
for spending our holidays. We were having a good
time and the city was giving us all what we expected.
When we arrived, we were having problems to find the
hotel, but a woman helped us and we got safe.
The days were passing by while we were having the

greatest time of our lives; we had the chance to try traditional food when we were visiting local markets. On the fifth day, we were having a great time at the beach when suddenly an alarm sounded…it was announcing that a tsunami was approaching. Everybody was running while we were trying to stay together in the middle of the terrible moment. Some minutes later, a big wave crashed over the land and lots of water was running over people while they were trying to escape… fortunately, we could get to high hill and survived.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
When we talk about actions happening in the past, we need to use the past progressive tense.
TO CONSIDER

We use the verb to be as auxiliary. In both forms: was / were.
The main verb takes the –ing form as seen in the examples. 
When is used to connect two ideas; in this case it presents an action that interrupts another one. 
While is used to state two actions happening simultaneously. 
Negative forms are wasn’t / weren’t.
Past Progressive tense
I was eating when the earthquake started.
Were you eating when the earthquake started?
They were relaxing at the beach when they gave the tsunami alert.
Were they relaxing at the beach when they gave the tsunami alert?
He was running fast while the tornado was chasing him.
Was he running fast while the tornado was chasing him?

texts: When we talk plans, we normally work in English using the “going to” structure. Check the following examples.
Going to is a fixed structure that denotes future.
The verbs after this grammatical structure go in simple form.
The future phrases at the end can be specific or general.
She is going to work as a community manager in the future.
Is she going to work as a community manager in the future?
They are going to become good traders at this rate.
Are they going to become good traders at this rate?
I am going to hitchhike so I can become a trip blogger.
Are you going to hitchhike so you can become a trip blogger?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
When we talk plans, we normally work in English using the “going to” structure. Check the following examples.
TO CONSIDER

Going to is a fixed structure that denotes future. 
The verbs after this grammatical structure go in simple form. 
 The future phrases at the end can be specific or general.
Going to
She is going to work as a community manager in the future.
Is she going to work as a community manager in the future?
They are going to become good traders at this rate.
Are they going to become good traders at this rate?
I am going to hitchhike so I can become a trip blogger.
Are you going to hitchhike so you can become a trip blogger?

texts: When we talk about life events or arrangements, we normally work in English using the present progressive structure. Check the following examples.
Using the present progressive with future phrases state future events likely to happen.
Phrases must state a definite moment mainly.
We are attending Joe’s wedding this Saturday.
Are you attending Joe’s wedding this Saturday?
They are graduating from college in some hours.
Are they graduating from college in some hours?
He is getting married in two days.
Is he getting married in two days?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
When we talk about life events or arrangements, we normally work in English using the present progressive structure. Check the following examples.
TO CONSIDER

Using the present progressive with future phrases state future events likely to happen. 
Phrases must state a definite moment mainly.
Be + Ving + Future Phrase
We are attending Joe’s wedding this Saturday.
Are you attending Joe’s wedding this Saturday?
They are graduating from college in some hours.
Are they graduating from college in some hours?
He is getting married in two days.
Is he getting married in two days?

texts: When we talk about  common life events we can use simple present and certain time phrases to state them in the future. Check the following examples.
Use the simple present plus phrases in future to state them ahead in time.
The phrases must reflect a close future.
I have a test this Tuesday.
Do you have a test this Tuesday?
They have to do laundry this weekend.
Do they have to do laundry this weekend?
He goes for his school performance tonight.
Does he go for his school performance tonight?

When we talk about  common life events we can use simple present and certain time phrases to state them in the future. Check the following examples.
TO CONSIDER

Use the simple present plus phrases in future to state them ahead in time. 
The phrases must reflect a close future. 
 Respect the simple present rules.
Simple Present + Future Phrase
I have a test this Tuesday.
Do you have a test this Tuesday?
They have to do laundry this weekend.
Do they have to do laundry this weekend?
He goes for his school performance tonight.
Does he go for his school performance tonight?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
When we talk about  weather we do not only use simple present. We can also use will. Check the following examples.
TO CONSIDER

Will is used to state future. 
Verbs go in simple form after using will. 
Future Time phrases are also needed.
Adverbs also help to state meaning.
Will – Future
It will rain soon. It is cloudy.
Will it rain soon?
It is cold; it will probably snow later.
Will it probably snow later?
Go fresh, it will be sunny at the beach.
Will it be sunny at the beach?

They have stayed in many lodges around the world.

They haven’t stayed in many lodges around the world.
There are also some adverbs that work with this structure
I have already been here for 6 hours.
She has just entered the hotel.
You have not called them yet.

texts: 1. Already – used to determine longer periods of time in actions.
2. Just – Used to determine shorter periods of time in actions.
3.  Yet –Used to state an actions has not occurred.
4. ALL of them can be in questions and sentences (yet only in questions and negative ones)
5. Have/Has are the auxiliaries. Main verbs must be in past participle.
6. There is a progressive tense that can be used here. E.G I have been waiting for the bus for two hours

texts: We can use present perfect tense to communicate different functions. Check out the following examples.
Express actions that started in the past and still continue.
They have visited us for two weeks already.
You have been tall since you were a child.
Talk about actions than happened only once or certain times.
He has just been there once.
We have stayed at your place many times.
We have been expecting him to change for so long.

-Why are you so tired? 
-I’ve been getting ready for the test all week.

3

We can talk about people’s behaviour and how they are supposed to act by using modals.
1. All verbs go in simple form after a modal.
2. Modals work with all pronouns with no problem.
3. Modals affect the main verbs according to the speaker's intention.
4. Would is also a common modal; You’ll hear more of it in an upcoming lesson.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph, extract sentences with the functions studied  and locate them in the space provided.

I always talk to myself, I find it interesting and refreshing. I know I should talk to other people for advise or just to share some of the things or situations I live, but it is very difficult. People have to be trustworthy and they need to prove themselves friend. “I should not look back into other bad experiences” I say to myself all the time; however, I must be clear too and I can’t be friends with everyone at first. People must give back what they receive and they should act towards others the same way others act towards them, but I guess not everyone thinks like me.

texts: We use indefinite pronouns to make generalizations about people, places and things.
1. All indefinite pronouns have a define connotation when using them.
2. The ones using “Any” mainly work in questions or negative sentences. However, it is possible to see them in positive sentences.
3. The ones using the particle “No” have already a full negative connotation like “never”.

texts: We use relative clauses or relative pronouns to include extra information about someone or something in the sentences.
Jake, who is the GOAT athlete, is here.
The club, where Sarah went legless, is closing.
The house, which the busybody bought, is great.
Tonight, when I see my jellybean, I’ll confess my love.
I don’t know why he is so wishy - washy about this.
Joe, whose party was so dismal, has another one this weekend.
1. Most relative pronouns are enclosed between commas.
2. They can also be used as the example with why.
3. How can be used to set clauses related to manners or ways.  E.G: I know how he did it!
4. We can also used that to create relative clauses for people and things.
Jane, that lives here, is my best friend.
The car, that is on the corner, was stolen yesterday.

texts: We may consider the relative clauses or pronouns as details we want or have to add to the information we already know. There are possible scenarios we can check out.
I don’t know why she didn’t come to the party.
My uncle was in the hospital where your aunt was operated.
These are not the only possible scenarios. Check out the following sentences:
I know someone who would love to see you!

*How can also be used here:
 I want to know how you did this (working as complement)
She did amazing , how she normally does, that night at the concert.(emphatic information)
All clauses can work like this

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We use relative clauses or relative pronouns to include extra information about someone or something in the sentences.
About...
Words
Examples
People
Who
Jake, who is the GOAT athlete, is here.
Places
Where
The club, where Sarah went legless, is closing.
Things
Which
The house, which the busybody bought, is great.
Time
When
Tonight, when I see my jellybean, I’ll confess my love.
Reasons
Why
I don’t know why he is so wishy - washy about this.
Belonging
Whose
Joe, whose party was so dismal, has another one this weekend.
To Consider
1. Most relative pronouns are enclosed between commas. 

2. They can also be used as the example with why. 

3. How can be used to set clauses related to manners or ways.  E.G: I know how he did it!
4. We can also used that to create relative clauses for people and things.

Jane, that lives here, is my best friend.
The car, that is on the corner, was stolen yesterday.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We may consider the relative clauses or pronouns as details we want or have to add to the information we already know. There are possible scenarios we can check out.
Scenarios
Examples
1
Emphasis
I don’t know why she didn’t come to the party.
2
Vague References
My uncle was in the hospital where your aunt was operated.
To consider

These are not the only possible scenarios. Check out the following sentences:

I know someone who would love to see you!

Remember what I told you.

*How can also be used here:
 I want to know how you did this (working as complement)
  She did amazing , how she normally does, that night at the concert.(emphatic information)
All clauses can work like this

texts: 1. Adjectives that finish in ING are used to describe situations or things.
2. Adjectives that finish in ED are used to describe how people feel because of something.
3.  Adjectives may be unique or classified into a pattern. E. G: Glib / Silly / Tiny
4. Some ING adjectives are used to describe people if they are producing something in someone else: I am annoyed, you know? Joey is so annoying, always talking too much.

texts: Although adjectives happen to be in a variety of contexts, their main function is to describe.
Describe situations or things that affect people.
I have to admit that was a fascinating lesson.
Describe how people feel by any situation or thing.
HAve you heard the story of the crooked man?

1. Some adjectives like crooked / naked do not follow the regular pronunciation rule for ED endings. This may be because of the origin of the word or because there is no corresponding verb to the adjective.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
To Consider 
1. Adjectives that finish in ING are used to describe situations or things.
2. Adjectives that finish in ED are used to describe how people feel because of something.
3.  Adjectives may be unique or classified into a pattern. E. G: Glib / Silly / Tiny
4. Some ING adjectives are used to describe people if they are producing something in someone else: I am annoyed, you know? Joey is so annoying, always talking too much.
slideDifferences.publishedText: To Consider 1. Adjectives that finish in -ING are normally used to describe situations or things. 2. Adjectives that finish in -ED are used to describe how people feel because of something. 3. Adjectives may be unique or classified into a pattern. E.G.: Glib / Silly / Tiny 4. Some -ING adjectives are used to describe people if they are producing something in someone else: I am annoyed, you know? Joey is so annoying, always talking too much. 5. Another issue is that some adjectives ending -IC and -ICAL tend to be confusing; here is a list for patterns https://www.thefreedictionary.com/Commonly-Confused-Suffixes-ic-vs-ical.htm#:~:text=The%20suffixes%20%E2%80%9C%2Dic%E2%80%9D%20and,are%20notoriously%20difficult%20to%20distinguish. https://www.thefreedictionary.com/Commonly-Confused-Suffixes-ic-vs-ical.htm#:~:text=The%20suffixes%20%E2%80%9C%2Dic%E2%80%9D%20and,are%20notoriously%20difficult%20to%20distinguish

texts: Conditionals may have a main purpose but they can receive a variety of functions.
If my dad catches us eating his chocolate, we are grounded for weeks.
Dilan gets upset when someone smokes in a public area.
Water boils if it reaches 100 degrees.
The sea gets high tides  if the moon is in a further range than it regularly is.

If you leave the room, turn the lights off.
Tell Jake to make his homework when you call him.
When giving instructions, the independent clause is mainly used in imperative form.

I know! People need to get some good manners nowadays.

texts: Conditionals link two different clauses as we learned in the last unit. First conditional links an action or circumstance in the present with another one in the future.
IF you get too much sun.
They need another clause to exist.

To Consider

The use of will is necessary since it is the way consequences in the future are expressed.
Sometimes, ‘can’ is also used to state a consequence. E.G: If you get wet under the rain, you can get a cold.
When the IF clause is the first one, it needs to be separated by a comma (,) from the other clause.

texts: We can use the first conditional aiming the following functions or aspects
Talking about illness and conditions people can get.
I will have to see a doctor if the fever continues.
If they do not operate him, he will lose his leg.
If Shane does not pass the course, he will be grounded for months.
The boys will not go to the party if they do not clean their room.
This two areas are not the only ones that can be covered. Generally, talking about consequences may be include the use of the conditional.

texts: They need another clause to exist.
Their parents would ground them for life.

To Consider

The use of would / could is commonly seen here to express the possibility about something.
The dependent clauses are used in simple past tense.
When the IF clause is the first one, it needs to be separated by a comma (,) from the other clause.
The correct form to use is: If I were...
Conditionals link two different clauses as we learned in the last unit. Second conditional links a possibility with a situation unlikely to happen.

She would definitely choose Mike if she ever got married.
I would say yes if I were her.
If he were a professional, they would probably hire him.

texts: Have you ever wondered what you would do if you were rich? I have. If I were rich, I would be using my money to start helping people and not by giving them money per se but giving the opportunities to study or prepare themselves. I would also open a foundation to help people develop their skills if they were willing to perfect and offer what they do. For sure, I would not use it just for that, but If I had enough money, I would definitely travel to meet new places and people. Haven’t you given a thought? If I were you, I would start considering it just in case.

Stop bothering your sister!

texts: B. Listen to the audio and answer the questions your teacher makes.

I am sure there are many conceptions on how to proceed in life regarding many issues. Fairly speaking, I believe people need to be honest to get along with others. Additionally, by respecting others, you can get to be respected as well. People have to understand that respect and honesty are fundamental to have and keep healthy relationships in life. I have decided to live by these standards and it would be a great idea for people to consider them, and have the courage to admit not having used these values in certain circumstances in order to say they’re sorry and mend what they did.
What do you think of this? Do you agree?

texts: When describing noses, you can use the adjectives hooked, pointy, flat, button.
Lips are describe as thin or thick. Also, full.
Eyebrows can also be described as thick, thin or bushy.

If you want to describe a piece of clothes, you need to follow the regular pattern of adjectives. The correct verb to use when talking about it is -wear- E.G. She is wearing a beautiful single red, silk, European nightgown. On top of it, she has a gorgeous, golden silk shawl.

When describing noses, you can use the adjectives hooked, pointy, flat, button. 
Lips are describe as thin or thick. Also, full.

texts:
I hate it…

She loves it…

I don’t mind it...

When someone runs late all the time.

When the kids play quietly.

When someone laughs out loud.

It upsets me…

It bothers my dad...

When my mums shouts for no reason.

When my little brother is noisy.

There are some other phrases that may be considered adverbial clauses as well.

Condition:  if / Unless / As if / Only if - You’ll get permission only if your father agrees.
Place: Everywhere / Wherever / Anywhere - Wherever I go, I see her.
Reason: Now that / Because / Since - You can start painting the room now that your brother is gone.
Among the ways we can express perspectives, we can consider the following structures.

I hate it when someone yells in public.
It upsets my mum when we do not clean our room.
State enjoyment in regards certain actions.
It brightens my days when someone thinks on me and texts me.
I love it when my kids help me with the housework.
Show you are ok with people’s doings.

John did not bring white cardboard but yellow.
I don’t mind the color as long as he brought one.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
STRUCTURES
IT CLAUSE
ADVERBIAL CLAUSE
1
It + Adverbial Clause
I hate it…

She loves it…

I don’t mind it...
When someone runs late all the time.

When the kids play quietly.

When someone laughs out loud.
2
It + Verb + Noun + Adverbial clause
It upsets me…

It bothers my dad...
When my mums shouts for no reason.

When my little brother is noisy.
There are some other phrases that may be considered adverbial clauses as well.

Condition:  if / Unless / As if / Only if - You’ll get permission only if your father agrees.
Place: Everywhere / Wherever / Anywhere - Wherever I go, I see her.
Reason: Now that / Because / Since - You can start painting the room now that your brother is gone.
Among the ways we can express perspectives, we can consider the following structures.

To Consider 
1. The other adverbial clauses are considered such since they can move within the sentences without affecting the meaning.
2. There are also adverbial clauses of time, contrast, comparison.
slideDifferences.publishedText: To Consider 1. The other adverbial clauses are considered such since they can move within the sentences without affecting the meaning. 2. There are also adverbial clauses of time, contrast, comparison: Time: Whenever you do that, I hate it! Contrast: Different from all we have seen, I still have one argument. Comparison: I am ok with all that as long as we all are safe.

There are some functions that we can cover when using the grammar learned in this unit.
Functions
Examples
1
Express disagreement towards certain actions.
I hate it when someone yells in public.

2
State enjoyment in regards certain actions.
It brightens my days when someone thinks on me and texts me.
I love it when my kids help me with the housework.
3
Show you are ok with people’s doings.
John did not bring white cardboard but yellow.
I don’t mind the color as long as he brought one.

texts: Most common modal to work with requests is would. However, there are other uses and modals that we can include here.
I would like a cheese cake.
Would you pass me the salt? Please.
She’d prefer to have a cold drink

To Consider

Would can also be used for offers. E.G.Would you like a cup of tea?
Can is also a modal that may be used for informal requests. E.G. Can I go to the bathroom?
Using will at the end of a sentence also implies a request. E.G. Stop bothering your sister, will you?
May is also used for formal request. E.G. May I say something?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Most common modal to work with requests is would. However, there are other uses and modals that we can include here.
MODALS TO USE
STATEMENTS
NOTES
1
WOULD
I would like a cheese cake.
Used to express wishes.
2
WOULD in questions.
Would you pass me the salt? Please.
Used to express requests.
3
WOULD + Prefer
She’d prefer to have a cold drink
Used to express preferences.
To Consider

Would can also be used for offers. E.G.Would you like a cup of tea?
Can is also a modal that may be used for informal requests. E.G. Can I go to the bathroom?
Using will at the end of a sentence also implies a request. E.G. Stop bothering your sister, will you?
May is also used for formal request. E.G. May I say something?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We can use would to express different ideas.
Functions
Examples
1
Expressing requests
Would you call Annie and tell her about the meeting?
2
Making offers
Would you like ice tea or hot coffee?
3
Establishing preferences
They’d prefer to stay home tonight.
4
Wishing
I’d love to get that scholarship.
To consider 
WOULD RATHER: It is used to state a choice. E.G:  I’d rather get a burger.
There are other uses of would but we will deal with them later on the program.
slideDifferences.publishedText: We can use would to express different ideas. Functions Examples 1 Expressing requests Would you call Annie and tell her about the meeting? 2 Making offers Would you like ice tea or hot coffee? 3 Establishing preferences They’d prefer to stay home tonight. 4 Wishing I’d love to get that scholarship. To consider Would also works with the adverbial particle rather. Generally, it is used to state you choose something / someone over another one. E.G: I’d rather take the red one, thanks. What would you rather do?

texts:
You realize about the differences in countries when you finally go and live somewhere else. That happened to me when I went to study in Taiwan. It is called the sleepless city since stores and business are supposed to stay open all night. Don’t get me wrong, I think it is acceptable to have some business and stores open, but all of them? Well, that is not the custom for us to have in my country. Normally, stores open in the morning and they closed at nights , so people are expected to go during that time; however, some folks are used to go 10 minutes before closing and I do believe you are not supposed to do that.

Have you had a similar experience?

slideDifferences.publishedText: I wasn’t prepared for the culture shock of being an international student For any student, moving away from home can be daunting. But I didn’t expect student life in Scotland to be all that different from my home of the Netherlands. After all, we get the same news and TV shows online. However, when I moved from Amsterdam to study at the University of Stirling, I began to realise that a few small things were catching me off balance. I was suffering a minor cultural shock. In my first year, I quickly found out my English was not as good as I had assumed. Most of my flatmates were born and raised in Scotland, and I constantly found myself having to ask people to repeat themselves. Their Scottish accents didn’t help and I was mispronouncing names and places all the time. I also got confused about small cultural things. Much to my flatmates’ amusement, it took me two Christmases to figure out that mince pies are not actually filled with minced beef. The language barrier meant that public transport was tricky at first. I found the lack of information about bus prices and how and where to get tickets really surprising. It turned a simple 15-minute journey into a daunting task. What a shift

I remember woman wearing decent elegant clothes most of the time back in my days. They used to wear good outfits that made them look great without showing anything. Now, there is a great difference. A lot of women wear clothes that show their bodies rather than conceal them; more and more women, specially the young ones, are considering that this should no be a problem since it is their bodies, a complete shift of what it used to be. However, some still maintain the firm conviction of looking great without showing and b doing so, they have become the rebels in a world that says differently. If they keep their conviction, they will probably inspire others in time, but the other side of the coin shows that many will turn towards the new shift.

slideDifferences.publishedText: How have women’s legal rights evolved over the last 50 years? Today, women have just three-quarters of the legal rights of men. In 1970, it was less than half. The Women, Business and the Law 2020 report presented results from our recent effort to document how laws have changed since 1970. This exceptional dataset has already facilitated ground-breaking research that shows that a country’s performance on the Women, Business and the Law index is associated with more women in the labor force, a smaller wage gap between men and women, and greater investments in health and education. We hope that sharing the data and reform descriptions on our website will lead to more evidence that will inspire policymakers to change their laws so that more women can contribute to economic growth and development. Analysis of 1,518 reforms across 50 years and 190 economies yields some interesting insights. First of all, significant progress has been made around the world. Second, the pace of reform has varied across regions. The high-income OECD and Sub-Saharan Africa regions have noted the biggest progress both in terms of volume of reforms and improvement in their average WBL index scores. The third interesting finding is that progress has been uneven across the eight different areas of the law measured by Women, Business and the Law. Most reforms were recorded in the areas of workplace protections and laws dealing with working parents. Despite the progress that has been made, more work remains. The modals are organized from the highest level to the lowest.

texts: It might not be possible to believe, but people could be able to change...at least if they want to. You may wonder what triggers changes in a person, but the truth is that it depends on every individual and the circumstances that surround him. Changes present challenges that might be difficult at the beginning but they may also bring good results. Everyone has faced difficulties and experiences that have made them grow and become a better version of themselves. Honestly, no one can say that changes are made in a wink, but the real issue is that they come for us to take advantage and evolve.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
What a shift

It might not be possible to believe, but people could be able to change...at least if they want to. You may wonder what triggers changes in a person, but the truth is that it depends on every individual and the circumstances that surround him. Changes present challenges that might be difficult at the beginning but they may also bring good results. Everyone has faced difficulties and experiences that have made them grow and become a better version of themselves. Honestly, no one can say that changes are made in a wink, but the real issue is that they come for us to take advantage and evolve.
C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences that present the language and functions studied.
slideDifferences.publishedText: People Can Change, But That Doesn't Mean They Will Most people agree: Everyone makes mistakes. You might use this phrase to console a loved one who’s done something they regret or boost self-compassion when you mess up yourself. Perhaps you add the reassurance, “You’ll do better next time,” or vow to use your experience to improve in the future. These common sayings imply people can change — and they absolutely can. Anyone can make an effort to alter specific habits or behaviors. Even some aspects of attitude and personality can change over time… with some dedicated effort. Yet while people can change, not everyone does. How can you tell if someone will ever really address certain behaviors? What factors make improvement more likely? Keep reading to find out. Change is often complicated, and it doesn’t always happen the way you envision. The following reminders can help you maintain a realistic perspective about the process. Article retrieved from: https://www.healthline.com/health/do-people-change https://www.healthline.com/health/do-people-change C. texts: If people are thinking that all good things will just land on their lap, they’d better start working on how they can get them. Life is not easy and we should learn how to cope with it intelligently so we get the most of it. You cannot always hit the nose on the head; there are times when you really feel lost or powerless. Nevertheless, hard situations make us grow and strengthen us to face challenges on daily basis. I truly think, we can take the most out of every situation if we really are looking forward to doing it. It intrigues me not to have everything set and at the same time it kind of scares me; however, There will always be something to do for solving any issue we may face.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Lemons in life!

If people are thinking that all good things will just land on their lap, they’d better start working on how they can get them. Life is not easy and we should learn how to cope with it intelligently so we get the most of it. You cannot always hit the nose on the head; there are times when you really feel lost or powerless. Nevertheless, hard situations make us grow and strengthen us to face challenges on daily basis. I truly think, we can take the most out of every situation if we really are looking forward to doing it. It intrigues me not to have everything set and at the same time it kind of scares me; however, There will always be something to do for solving any issue we may face.
C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences that present the language and functions studied.
slideDifferences.publishedText: Successful Managers Know That Luck Goes With Effort Experienced managers learn that success is a combination of luck and effort. Arrogant and inexperienced managers may think any success is entirely from effort. They’d better change that idea. Anyone who works in management long enough will see many managers rise and fall according to their measures of luck and effort. Some of the managers who fall end up rising again through ambition and perseverance while others do not. Firings, demotions, layoffs and personal problems derail many careers. The ones who bounce back, lick their wounds and find a way to rise once more so they can superpass whatever makes them fall. The most successful managers have exceptional traits including higher than average intelligence, character, ambition, energy and leadership skills. But luck does play a part. Even they can’t control everything or guarantee success in any and all situations; shouldn’t this be something to think of? For example, a senior manager who took over a struggling operation couldn’t do anything about a key subordinate who sadly was dying of leukemia. Nor could he do anything about other underperforming business units that were dragging down the entire division, which ultimately led to its demise. slideDifferences.nativeText:
Grammar
Examples
Observation
1
Preferences + Non finite clauses.
I need someone to build a life with. 

Any woman needs a good guy devoted to share her life.

Being ethical and committed, Paul wishes to get the same from his employees.
Non Finite clause are built from:

-Infinitive Clauses
-Ed Clauses.
-Ing Clauses
2
Preferences + Relative clauses.
Josh would love a company that can value his talent. 

Mary fancies a car where she can fit all her friends. 

I’m desperate for a partner who can meet my professional standards.
Relative clauses need to respect their principles even here.
Preference can have an extended meaning if we use the more complex grammar points to regular ones.
slideDifferences.publishedText: Grammar Examples Observation 1 Preferences + Non-finite clause I need someone to build a life with. Any woman needs a good guy devoted to share his life with her. Being ethical and committed, Paul wishes to get the same from his employees. Non-finite clauses are built from: -Infinitive Clauses -Past participle Clauses -ing Clauses 2 Preferences + Relative clause Josh would love a company that can value his talent. Mary fancies a car where she can fit all her friends. I’m desperate for a partner who can meet my professional standards. Relative clauses need to respect their principles even here. Preference can have an extended meaning if we use the more complex grammar points to regular ones.

To Consider 
1. Rather than is also another particle we use to build a non finite clause. E.G. Rather than leave the child alone, I brought him to work with me. 
2. We can also use small clauses. E.G. Her face all red with shame, she expressed what she wanted. 
3. We can also use It clauses. E.G. I love it when people are polite. 
*Verb must be in simple form.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Preferences can be expressed in any tense and we the use of the correct clauses we can advocate the following functions.
Functions
Examples
1
State what people look for and want from others.
They’d love us to dance by their music during the training.
I expect committed classmates who make big efforts.
2
Express what you look for and want from things / situations
Striving through problems, the company desires the employees to stick by it.
Ashamed and disgusted, Jake wanted the problem to be over so he came clean.
To consider 
1. Clauses are not only used for this. We can use clauses in any other context as long as we are logical and coherent.

texts: B. Listen to the audio and answer the questions your teacher makes.

It is very common to listen to people say: If you want to do something, do it yourself. Have others make chores or favors for / to you does not always end well. Get people to work or do things  the way you want has always been kind of a challenge. If we refer to a professional area, you need to have people trained so they know what you want and expect. On a more personal level, get others to know you and get to know them will make things easier in dealing with different situations that may present. Whatever it is, professional or personal, have others do things for us or get things done by others is something challenging.

texts: 1. Verb + Preposition combination receive the stress on the verb particle.
2. Verb + Adverb combination receives the stress on the adverb particle.
3. Verb + Adverb + Preposition combination receives the stress on the adverb particle
4. Some phrasal verbs may be separable. That is to say, the object goes in the middle of the particles. This mainly happens when the object is a pronoun. E.G. We need to call it off.
5. Separable phrasal verbs work also together. E.G. We called off the meeting.

Look at the information, listen to your teacher and repeat the expressions. Discuss about them.
IDIOM
MEANING
EXAMPLE
GET ON THE BANDWAGON
To join an activity that has become very popular.
The success of the product led many firms to try to get on the bandwagon.
KEEP THE CHIN UP
To be stalwart and courageous in a tough situation.
Don't let the difficulties intimidate you; keep your chin up.
WALK OUT ON
To suddenly leave a job, a relationship or other situation.
Everyone was shocked when he walked out on his wife of fourteen year.
COME OUT SWINGING
To be confrontational.
He came out swinging at his critics, accusing them of having their own agenda.
BEEF UP
To become big and muscular.
We need to find some new players to beef up the team.
TURN ASIDE
To refuse entry to somewhere.
His job application was turned aside when they saw his criminal record.
TIDE OVER
Temporary help (often financial)
Have another piece of cake. It'll tide you over till supper.
CRACK UP
Go through an emotional breakdown.
The entire group cracked up at the joke of their teacher.

texts: 1. Have– used to talk about food, drink, washing, resting talking.
2. Take – Used to talk about washing, resting, decisions, problems, care.
4. Go - Used with verbs to do with moving. Also, with nouns that do not have an ing form, we use the structure ‘go for a’
5. Do - Used with nouns in ing that have to do with work. Additionally, with nouns when it is obvious what the action is.
6. Give - Used with noises, facial expressions, hittings, affectionate actions, talking.
7. Adjectives are used to add extra information to the action we want to express.

Extend meaning through common word actions.

I need to go for a walk.

She gave me a huge smile.

We will have a light dinner tonight.

In most cases, there is a verb that has a meaning similar or equal to the delexical structure. These structures are very common in English and an understanding of them will enrich the fluency of the language.

texts: B. Listen to the audio and answer the questions your teacher makes.

I work for a global IT company, but because their headquarters is in the States, I do all my work online from home. That means that I don't waste time commuting or making idle chit-chat with colleagues. I work on a project basis, and this flexibility is very valuable to me because it means that I can easily take some time off when my children need me to go to their school performances or if I need to make an appointment with the dentist. The downside is that without clear office hours, I tend to work well into the evening, sometimes without having dinner to finish a task. It can also get quite lonely working on my own, and I sometimes miss sharing ideas with colleagues.

IDIOM
MEANING
EXAMPLE
GIVE SOMETHING A SHOT
To have a try at something.
I have never eaten sushi, but I will give it a shot.
HAVE A BONE TO PICK
An unpleasant issue or grievance that need discussion.
I have a bone to pick with you about that email.
GO FOR BROKE
To risk everything and go for an all out effort.
If you decide to go for broke, you can’t be thinking about what will happen if you fail.
MAKE A CLEAN SWEEP
To remove all unwanted people or things in order to start afresh.
The new leaders wanted to make a clean sweep of the discredited old order
GIVE THE NOD
To show one's approval of someone or something.
I gave Amanda the nod because she is the most qualified candidate.
HAVE AN AX TO GRIND
To have a private reason for doing or being involved in something.
He has no political axe to grind.
GO-TO GUY/GAL
The person is frequently asked for help in that topic.
Amanda’s our go-to gal for computer issues.
MAKE A KILLING
To earn a lot of money in a short time and with little effort.
They made a killing with the sale of their London house.
Look at the information, listen to your teacher and repeat the words. Discuss about them.

B. Listen to the audio and answer the questions your teacher makes.
Work-life balance

I work for a global IT company, but because their headquarters is in the States, I do all my work online from home. That means that I don't waste time commuting or making idle chit-chat with colleagues. I work on a project basis, and this flexibility is very valuable to me because it means that I can easily take some time off when my children need me to go to their school performances or if I need to make an appointment with the dentist. The downside is that without clear office hours, I tend to work well into the evening, sometimes without having dinner to finish a task. It can also get quite lonely working on my own, and I sometimes miss sharing ideas with colleagues.

Adapted from https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/skills/reading/upper-intermediate-b2/work-life-balance

texts: To lose one’s temper by shooting words.
My dad went ballistic when he found out we had a party in the house.
Then, I knew she had just made me livid.
To become very angry about something.
My dad just blew my mum’s top when she knew he had not paid the hall for the party.
I am just cross with her now!
To reply sharply and brusquely to someone.
The teacher just bit all students’ heads for the problem they caused.
To describe a person that suddenly gets really angry.
Every time someone talks about the changes in the school policy, Jessica flies off the handle.
If the boss comes back and we aren’t done with this, he is going to blow a gasket.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

texts: 1. Past Perfect + By uses normally a noun phrase after the preposition.
2. Past Perfect + Before uses normally a clause in simple past after the
3. Past Perfect + When uses normally a clause in simple past after the
4. If we talk about one single event, there’s no need for us to use past perfect. E.G. Romans had spoken Latin. The correct form is: Romans spoke Latin.

5.  We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. 
Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework.
-Totally, Mrs. Swan. Jax had already done his homework when you called.

texts: We can use past perfect to talk about the following aspects.
Express actions that time up to a point in the past.
They had already moved three times by the end of 2020.
Talk about undone or incomplete actions in the past.
Before he went ballistic, I had delivered what he wanted.
State actions that already happened before others in the past.
When the police came into the building, The gang had already stolen everything.
In most cases, already can be the adverb to use; however, ever and never can suit depending on the context.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with the delexical verbs and tell your teacher what is their intended meaning.

Hi, have you ever had one of those days when everything seemed to go wrong? I'm sure you have, I know I have. I remember one particular day, I'd been invited to a party and there was someone going who I'd never met but I really wanted to meet, so I was quite excited about going to this party, and I maybe spent too long getting ready and I was a bit late when I was leaving the house, but not too late. But then I looked down and saw I had a hole in my tights! So I had to go back inside, change my tights, come out again, so I was getting a little bit late for the party, but not too bad. I got in my car, started driving, about halfway to the party my car stopped.

I couldn't understand what was the matter until I looked at the petrol gauge: it had run out of petrol! Why? Because I'd lent my car to my son the day before and he'd used the petrol and he hadn't filled the car up! So I thought I'd ring the AA. I looked in my handbag to find my mobile phone, but I couldn't find it. Why? Because I'd left it next to my bed charging. So even though it was pouring with rain, I had to get out of my car, in my party clothes, walk to the petrol station and come back with petrol.

By which time I was nearly 2 hours late. So, I was so flustered about being late, I started to drive and I just took a wrong turn and I ended up on this one-way system, totally lost, driving round and round for at least 45 minutes before I managed to get my bearings. So finally, I arrived at the party over 3 hours late and when I arrived the person I wanted to meet had just left, all the food had gone, and my host was horribly drunk. I was so disappointed that I just turned around and left and went back home. Have you ever had a terrible day like that, when everything went wrong? If you have, write and tell us about it.

Structures
EXAMPLES
SWITCHING CLAUSES
Had + Past participle + by
Jake had already published his first book by the age of 20.
By the age of 20, Jake had already published his first book.
Had + Past participle + before
The boss had bitten everyone’s head off before I got with the answer.
before I got with the answer, the boss had bitten everyone’s head off.
Had + Past participle + when
Jazmin had already had a fit when HH.RR. solved the problem.
when HH.RR. solved the problem, Jazmin had already had a fit
.There is another way to use past perfect using If clauses to talk about unreal situations in the past:
If I had known, I would have told you. (Unit 45 will explained all about that)
When we work with past tense, we can also talk about things that had already happen or taken place before others. We use past perfect for tha.
slideDifferences.publishedText: Structures EXAMPLES SWITCHING CLAUSES Had + Past participle + by Jake had already published his first book by the age of 20. By the age of 20, Jake had already published his first book. Had + Past participle + before The boss had bitten everyone’s head off before I got with the answer. Before I got with the answer, the boss had bitten everyone’s head off. Had + Past participle + when Jazmin had already had a fit when HR solved the problem. When HR solved the problem, Jazmin had already had a fit. .There is another way to use past perfect using If clauses to talk about unreal situations in the past: If I had known, I would have told you. (Unit 45 will explain all about that). Past perfect can also be used in questions and negative sentences. When we work with past tense, we can also talk about things that had already happened or taken place before others. We use past perfect for that.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
To Consider 
1. Past Perfect + By uses normally a noun phrase after the preposition. 
2. Past Perfect + Before uses normally a clause in simple past after the 
    preposition. 
3. Past Perfect + When uses normally a clause in simple past after the 
    preposition.  
4. If we talk about one single event, there’s no need for us to use past perfect. E.G. Romans had spoken Latin. The correct form is: Romans spoke Latin.
5.  We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. 
Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework.
                -Totally, Mrs. Swan. Jax had already done his homework when you called.

We can use a past perfect clause alone when the context is already known. E.G. Context: A mum asked by phone if her son did his homework. -Totally, Mrs. Swan. texts: To talk socially without exchanging too much information.
Be careful! Just shoot the breeze.
To meddle in someone else’s business.
Dean is such a nosy parker; always snooping around.
A story that is not true or that lacks of details.
That guy always with his pork pies; we need a new janitor.
To divulge something that we are not certain to be true.
I heard Mary left John, but I think our neighbors are just spinning the yarn.
To speak about others and reveal secrets or intimacies.

To Consider

Most of the structures we know change when we use reported or indirect speech.
Most common verbs to use to report are: Say, Tell and Ask as you see in the examples. 
The particle that is commonly used at the beginning of the report; but it can be omitted to. 
The word if is used when we are reporting a question as shown in the examples. 
The modals Should, Could, Must and ought maintain their original form in reported speech; like Might and Would, they DO NOT CHANGE.

texts: We can use indirect speech for the following functions:
They told us they had already finished the project.
Jane asked Joe if he could buy dinner on his way home.
Carlos asked me to help him out.
When reporting requests, we normally used the verb ASK. Also, when doing it, we work with INFINITIVE FORMS as you see in the example.
Requests can be negative too. E.G.
Please, don’t smoke here. ---------> She asked me NOT to smoke here.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with reported speech; what are they reporting? After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
She said she loved me: A Case of a Crime of Passion.

After 35 years, the police department in our city has finally solved the mysterious death of the famous business woman Regina Mills. The chief of the department said that they had discovered a piece of evidence that had been overlooked years ago. That evidence directed them to Mrs. Mills’ husband, Frederick Thwan. Apparently, there was a note from the deceased that was not found  until two weeks ago after her death anniversary where Mr. Smith, from the international bank, publicly told the press they had sustained an affair and claimed he had found a note from his lover saying, and we quote, He knows. Mr. Smith asked the police to reopen the case and he said that he would not stop until getting the responsible one. After 3 weeks or so of the reopening, the police linked the evidence to Mr. Thawn who confessed doing it and told the police he had done it because she said she loved him but it was not true. The case was finally closed and the police told the citizenry Mr. Thwn would never see the sun again.

May 27th, 2021.

After 35 years, the police department in our city has finally solved the mysterious death of the famous business woman Regina Mills. Apparently, there was a note from the deceased that was not found  until two weeks ago after her death anniversary where Mr. Smith, from the international bank, publicly told the press they had sustained an affair and claimed he had found a note from his lover saying, and we quote, He knows. Mr. Smith asked the police to reopen the case and he said that he would not stop until getting the responsible one. After 3 weeks or so of the reopening, the police linked the evidence to Mr. Thawn who confessed doing it and told the police he had done it because she said she loved him but it was not true. The case was finally closed and the police told the citizenry Mr. Thwn would never see the sun again. 
Roberts, J.

REPORTED SPEECH

Modals
I can go with you. 
We would help you.
I may not go.
We might have a review.
He told me he could go with us.
They told us they would help us.
He said that he might not go.

To Consider

Most of the structures we know change when we use reported or indirect speech.
Most common verbs to use to report are: Say, Tell and Ask as you see in the examples. 
The particle that is commonly used at the beginning of the report; but it can be omitted to. 
The word if is used when we are reporting a question as shown in the examples. 
The modals Should, Could, Must and ought maintain their original form in reported speech; like Might and Would, they DO NOT CHANGE.

Functions
Examples

To Consider

Tag questions are used at the end of the sentences.
Tag questions are used to with any tense as you see in the examples. 
If the statement is positive, the tag question goes negative. 
If the statement is negative, the tag question goes positive. 
If the subject is ‘I’, the tag questions works with aren’t. E.G. I am right, aren’t I?
Using the expression Let’s makes us work with the word shall. E.G. Let’s go, shall we?
When having Imperatives, we work with will. E.G. Close the door, will you?
Affirmative tags after affirmative statements can be used to express interest or surprise. E.G You are leaving home, are you?

texts: We can use tag questions for the following functions:

You can’t swim, can you?
They are not coming, are they?

The food was delicious, wasn’t it?
You love this movie, don’t you?

They were married, weren’t they?
You have not told them, have you?

You made this draft, did you?
You had planned it all, had you?
If you pronounce the tag question with a rising intonation, the utterance will declare uncertainty.
If you pronounce the tag question with falling intonation, the utterance will declare certainty; you just need confirmation.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with tag questions. What function are they representing. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
You know what it means, don’t you?

It would be definitely amazing if we spoke at least three or four languages naturally, wouldn’t it? However, the reality is that most people are exposed to two languages or three as a top when being kids which means that acquiring others would take time and dedication during life. Additionally, we all need to understand that learning a language requires a big effort and that it will not come out of the blue won’ t it? For instance, attending classes and looking for professional help are the first steps we have to take into account, but there is also the need for giving ourselves the chance to practice outside classes, opening spaces where we are in touch with the language and of course use what we learn.

However, there are many who think that just attending lessons is enough, don’t they? Also,  that there is no need to listen or to check what there was in my previous lesson in order to acquire a good level. Sadly, thinking like that only leads to self - frustration  since those people learn the hard way that learning a language means so much more than coming to class, doesn’t it?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
A FUSS
A display of unnecessary or excessive excitement, activity, or interest.
I don't know what all the fuss is about.
A SCAM
A deceptive scheme or trick used to cheat someone out of something, especially money.
The buy of the cars turned out to be just a scam.
A STORM IN A TEACUP
A small event that has been exaggerated out of proportion.
It was not that serious. Stom making a storm in a teacup.
A CHARADE
An absurd pretense intended to create a pleasant or respectable appearance.
I will ask Tina to cut the charade off.
A LIP SERVICE
An expression of agreement that is not supported by real conviction
We cannot believe for a second the lip service given by the candidate.
A SNOW JOB
A deception or a fraud
It is all a snow job, isn’t it?
A SHARP PRACTICE
A deceitful sneaky practice.
After the sharp practice was discovered the government has been keeping a closer eye on the private sector.
A FISH TALE
A lie or an exaggeration of the truth.
I don’t think he was telling the truth, it sounded like nothing but a good old fish tale to me.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

texts: AT THE BACK OF YOUR MIND
Something that you are not thinking about right now but is in your thoughts.
At the back of my mind is the fear of failing the exam.
An idea which constantly occupies your thoughts.
Eva's got a bee in her bonnet about moving to New York.
It refers to an imaginary unrealistic place where everything is perfect and impossible things can happen.
It was not that serious. Stom making a storm in a teacup.
It means that something  is very imaginative but not at all practical or sensible.
Jimmy often has good ideas but his latest proposal is just a flight of fancy!
A sudden moment of inspiration, comprehension or realisation.
Harry had a light-bulb moment when he finally realised what was blocking the mechanism.
Bear in mind that no food will be served on board.
IT means not to seriously think about something.
Sally has often toyed with the idea of moving abroad, but she's still here!
When something is just product of your imagination. It is not real.
Don't be silly. Nobody is trying to harm you. It's all in your head!

We use passive voice when we want to explain how something is done, what it is made of and who has done it.

texts: The boys are painting the house.
The house is being painted by the boys.
She was preparing dinner for us.
Dinner was being prepared for us.

To Consider

In active voice, we focus on who / what makes the action but in passive voice the focus goes on the object.
It is considered to be used in formal contexts; however, its use is very common.
In passive voice, the who / what makes the action can be omitted. 
In perfect tenses, we need to add the word been before the participle.
The most common progressive tenses using passive voice are present and past.
When using present and past progressive, we use the verb to be + being + the participle.
Perfect progressive tenses may also work with passive voice; however, they are not very common. E.G. Our music has been annoying the man next door - The man next door has been being annoyed by our music.

To Consider

In active voice, we focus on who / what makes the action but in passive voice the focus goes on the object.
It is considered to be used in formal contexts; however, its use is very common.
In passive voice, the who / what makes the action can be omitted. 
In perfect tenses, we need to add the word been before the participle.
The most common progressive tenses using passive voice are present and past.
When using present and past progressive, we use the verb to be + being + the participle.
Perfect progressive tenses may also work with passive voice; however, they are not very common. E.G. Our music has been annoying the man next door - The man next door has been being annoyed by our music.

texts: We can use passive voice for the following functions:
State what things are made of

The legs of the table are iron-made.
The spoon was handcrafted in wood.
Declare when things are made / done.

The meeting will be set for tomorrow.
Is this piano being played this week?
Point who things are made / done by.

They were married, weren’t they?
You have not told them, have you?
Focus on objects rather than subjects in general actions.

Why was my burger eaten from the fridge?
Five points will be taken from your test for cheating.
Passive voice is not only used for the first three asécts; It can also be implemented in regular actions or everyday matters.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and identify the sentences in passive voice. What function are they representing. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.

The shipping industry says it's been hit by the global financial crisis and the recent spate of piracy attacks off Somalia. The chairman of the Hong Kong Ship Owners Association and chief executive of the Anglo-Eastern Group, Peter Cremers said ships are wary of sailing through the Gulf of Aden which has boosted costs as vessels are diverted.

Analysts polled by Reuters news agency say they believe China's economy grew by just seven per cent in the last quarter of last year. If borne out by official data, this would be the worst figure in a decade. The Chinese authorities believe a minimum growth rate of eight per cent is needed to avoid severe unemployment and social disruption. China's manufacturing sector has been badly hit by recession in its main export markets.

Temperatures over Hong Kong dipped on Sunday morning with the mercury plunging to minus one degree celsius in Ta Kwu Ling. A spokesman for the Observatory said it was the lowest temperature recorded in Ta Kwu Ling since a weather station was set up there,  more than two decades ago. The Observatory says the average temperature recorded in the urban areas was 10 degrees. But, it was considerably colder in some parts of the New Territories.
