slideDifferences.nativeText:
PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
AT THE BACK OF YOUR MIND
Something that you are not thinking about right now but is in your thoughts.
At the back of my mind is the fear of failing the exam.
A BEE IN ONE’S BONNET
An idea which constantly occupies your thoughts.
Eva's got a bee in her bonnet about moving to New York.
LIVE / BE CLOUD CUCKOO
It refers to an imaginary unrealistic place where everything is perfect and impossible things can happen.
It was not that serious. Stom making a storm in a teacup.
A FLIGHT OF FANCY
It means that something  is very imaginative but not at all practical or sensible.
Jimmy often has good ideas but his latest proposal is just a flight of fancy!
A LIGHT BULB MOMENT
A sudden moment of inspiration, comprehension or realisation.
Harry had a light-bulb moment when he finally realised what was blocking the mechanism.
BEAR/KEEP IN MIND
To remember something.
Bear in mind that no food will be served on board.
TOY WITH THE IDEA
IT means not to seriously think about something.
Sally has often toyed with the idea of moving abroad, but she's still here!
BE ALL IN YOUR HEAD
When something is just product of your imagination. It is not real.
Don't be silly. Nobody is trying to harm you. It's all in your head!
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
STRUCTURES
ACTIVE VOICE
PASSIVE VOICE
To be + Past Participle
They build the building in glass.
The building is built in glass.
Someone stole my car yesterday.
My car was stolen yesterday.
Those are plastic chairs.
Those chairs are plastic-made.
To be + Past Participle + by
Alex will finish the job tonight.
The job will be finished by Alex tonight.
John has done the house chores lately.
The house chores have been done by John lately.
Tim had borne in mind this idea for ages.
This idea had been borne in mind by Tim for ages.
We use passive voice when we want to explain how something is done, what it is made of and who has done it.

texts: We are able to express ideas about things that never came to happen in the past by using the third conditional. Check the chart.
Would  Have + Past Participle + If clause.
Joe would have come to his senses if she had been honest at first.
Would Joe have come to his senses if she had been honest at first?
The movie would not definitely have gone bad if they had kept the hunky dory story from the very beginning.
Would the movie ever have gone bad?
If clause + Would have + Past Participle
If they had not gone off the wall, we would have probably closed that contract.
What if they had not gone off the walls?
If Jake had sought carefully, the investigation would have not turned out a failure.
How would have the investigation turned out if Jake had sought carefully?

To Consider
Would have is the auxiliary of this structure.
The if clause used here must go in past perfect. 
Adverbs can be used here as they are used for other structures. 
We need to use a comma when the if clause goes first. 
We can use any interrogative words to make questions.
Indirect questions are possible as shown in the examples.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.

The sinking of the RMS Titanic was one of the worst maritime disasters in history. On April 14, 1912, at 11:40 p.m., the ‘unsinkable’ luxury ship hit an iceberg and sank in just under three hours with the loss of around 1500 lives. There are many different descriptions of the disaster by the surviving passengers and crew, but few people doubt that human error played a part in the tragedy. Let’s look at some of the things that went wrong.
On the night of Sunday, 14 April 1912 the temperature was near freezing and the ocean was
completely calm. Surviving 2nd Officer Charles Lightoller later wrote, "the sea was like glass". The

ship’s course had been changed by the captain, but other than this, he saw no reason to slow down.The owner of the ship, Bruce Ismay, was also on board and had instructed the captain to speed up in order to break the record for a transatlantic voyage. The captain agreed, but perhaps if he had known of the messages the ship had received in the radio room, he would have  acted differently. According to a ship ahead called the Mesaba, lots of large icebergs were in the area. These messages did not reach him.

There were three teams of lookouts on board keeping constant watch for obstacles in the ship’s path, but as Charles Lightoller said at the British inquiry, "Everything was against us, there was no moon, no wind, no binoculars and with the dark side of the iceberg facing the ship, the lookouts were powerless.”

The sinking of the RMS Titanic was one of the worst maritime disasters in history. On April 14, 1912, at 11:40 p.m., the ‘unsinkable’ luxury ship hit an iceberg and sank in just under three hours with the loss of around 1500 lives. There are many different descriptions of the disaster by the surviving passengers and crew, but few people doubt that human error played a part in the tragedy. Let’s look at some of the things that went wrong.

On the night of Sunday, 14 April 1912 the temperature was near freezing and the ocean was
completely calm. Surviving 2nd Officer Charles Lightoller later wrote, "the sea was like glass". The
ship’s course had been changed by the captain, but other than this, he saw no reason to slow down.The owner of the ship, Bruce Ismay, was also on board and had instructed the captain to speed up in order to break the record for a transatlantic voyage. The captain agreed, but perhaps if he had known of the messages the ship had received in the radio room, he would have  acted differently. According to a ship ahead called the Mesaba, lots of large icebergs were in the area. These messages did not reach him. 

There were three teams of lookouts on board keeping constant watch for obstacles in the ship’s path, but as Charles Lightoller said at the British inquiry, "Everything was against us, there was no moon, no wind, no binoculars and with the dark side of the iceberg facing the ship, the lookouts were powerless.”

texts: When the alarm was finally raised the crew acted very quickly but it was already too late to save the ship. Within twenty minutes of the collision the ship had flooded, so the captain ordered the lifeboats to be prepared, filled with women and children, and lowered into the water. This didn’t go well, regulations about the number of lifeboats a ship should carry were already out of date when the Titanic set sail, and even if the evacuation had been better organised, there wouldn’t have been enough boats to hold everybody.
Meanwhile, the crew were sending out distress signals. The first message was "sinking, need
immediate assistance," and then "SOS". Several ships responded, including the Mount Temple,
Frankfurt, and the Titanic's sister ship, Olympic, but they were too far away. The closest ship to
respond was the Carpathia, which arrived in about four hours, too late to save everybody.

Various distress flares launched from the sinking ship were also ineffective, including those seen by a ship called the Californian, whose captain, Stanley Lord, had ordered his crew to stop the ship for the  night because of the icebergs. When Captain Lord was informed of the flares he failed to respond because he did not think they were important. Nor did the crew of the Californian wake their radio operator, who had gone to bed for the night.
And what of Bruce Ismay, who many believe acted without regard for safety by requiring an
unprepared ship to sail at such speed in spite of the danger? History tells us that he survived, but from the lifeboat turned his back on his beautiful ship as it sank

That night, of a total of 2,208 people, only 712 were rescued by the Carpathia, while 1,496 perished. If the lifeboats had been filled to capacity, 1,178 people could have been saved. If there had been enough lifeboats, maybe everybody could have been saved. However, we may never know for sure.

PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
ONCE IN A BLUE MOON
Something that is rare. Events that are not as common as some others.
Once in a blue moon, Pete gets good grades.
TWELFTH OF NEVER
Something that will never come to pass.
If they had called Jane, this wouldn’t definitely  have gone twelfth of the never.
FEW AND FAR BETWEEN
Events that are odd or rarely seen.
John calling? That is quite a few and far between.
A COLD DAY IN HELL
It means that something can’t be possible as hell going cold.
Hell would have gone on a cold day if Dinah had arrived on time.
BEYOND BELIEF
Something so great or terrible to be true
That would've been beyond belief if they had prepared the play themselves.
HUNKY DORY
It may be understood as something out of this world or wicked.
The presentations was pretty hunky dory, congrats!
A NO GO
It means something is worthless or unreal.
It all would have been a no go if Mark had not stood up before the committee.
OFF THE WALL
When something is just strange or weird.
The new poster is just off the wall.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We are able to express ideas about things that never came to happen in the past by using the third conditional. Check the chart.
STRUCTURES
STATEMENTS
QUESTIONS
Would  Have + Past Participle + If clause.
Joe would have come to his senses if she had been honest at first.
Would Joe have come to his senses if she had been honest at first?
The movie would not definitely have gone bad if they had kept the hunky dory story from the very beginning.
Would the movie ever have gone bad?
If clause + Would have + Past Participle
If they had not gone off the wall, we would have probably closed that contract.
What if they had not gone off the walls?
If Jake had sought carefully, the investigation would have not turned out a failure.
How would have the investigation turned out if Jake had sought carefully?
To Consider
Would have is the auxiliary of this structure.
The if clause used here must go in past perfect. 
Adverbs can be used here as they are used for other structures. 
We need to use a comma when the if clause goes first. 
We can use any interrogative words to make questions.
Indirect questions are possible as shown in the examples.

There are many different descriptions of the disaster by the surviving passengers and crew, but few people doubt that human error played a part in the tragedy. Let’s look at some of the things that went wrong. On the night of Sunday, 14 April 1912 the temperature was near freezing and the ocean was completely calm. Surviving 2nd Officer Charles Lightoller later wrote, "the sea was like glass". The ship’s course had been changed by the captain, but other than this, he saw no reason to slow down.The owner of the ship, Bruce Ismay, was also on board and had instructed the captain to speed up in order to break the record for a transatlantic voyage. The captain agreed, but perhaps if he had known of the messages the ship had received in the radio room, he would have acted differently. According to a ship ahead called the Mesaba, lots of large icebergs were in the area. These messages did not reach him. There were three teams of lookouts on board keeping constant watch for obstacles in the ship’s path, but as Charles Lightoller said at the British inquiry, "Everything was against us, there was no moon, no wind, no binoculars and with the dark side of the iceberg facing the ship, the lookouts were powerless.”

slideDifferences.nativeText:
‹#›
When the alarm was finally raised the crew acted very quickly but it was already too late to save the ship. Within twenty minutes of the collision the ship had flooded, so the captain ordered the lifeboats to be prepared, filled with women and children, and lowered into the water. This didn’t go well, regulations about the number of lifeboats a ship should carry were already out of date when the Titanic set sail, and even if the evacuation had been better organised, there wouldn’t have been enough boats to hold everybody. 

Meanwhile, the crew were sending out distress signals. The first message was "sinking, need
immediate assistance," and then "SOS". Several ships responded, including the Mount Temple,
Frankfurt, and the Titanic's sister ship, Olympic, but they were too far away. The closest ship to
respond was the Carpathia, which arrived in about four hours, too late to save everybody. 

Various distress flares launched from the sinking ship were also ineffective, including those seen by a ship called the Californian, whose captain, Stanley Lord, had ordered his crew to stop the ship for the  night because of the icebergs. When Captain Lord was informed of the flares he failed to respond because he did not think they were important. Nor did the crew of the Californian wake their radio operator, who had gone to bed for the night.

And what of Bruce Ismay, who many believe acted without regard for safety by requiring an
unprepared ship to sail at such speed in spite of the danger? History tells us that he survived, but from the lifeboat turned his back on his beautiful ship as it sank

That night, of a total of 2,208 people, only 712 were rescued by the Carpathia, while 1,496 perished. If the lifeboats had been filled to capacity, 1,178 people could have been saved. If there had been enough lifeboats, maybe everybody could have been saved. However, we may never know for sure.

James Corden, host of the reunion that we all couldn't stop talking about, recruited the cast of "Friends" for a special segment that aired on his show Wednesday night.

In the clip, Corden helps transport the cast -- Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc, Matthew Perry and David Schwimmer -- to the set and uses the brief ride through the Warner Bros. lot, where they used to film, to channel "Carpool Karaoke." Do you really need to ask the song choice? We all would have chosen the same, wouldn’t we?

After belting The Rembrandt's "I'll Be There For You," Corden and the cast get cozy in Central Perk for some fun and games, that turns some on the couches to tears as we all must’ve expected. "Friends: The Reunion" was released last month on HBO Max. (CNN, like HBO, is owned by WarnerMedia.) and it was said to be the last episode (reunion) of the cast despite fans would have desired it to be one of many to come.

While the streamer has not released viewing numbers, Variety reported that the highly-anticipated special may have performed nearly as well as "Wonder Woman 1984," the sequel to the 2017 blockbuster superhero film. Nevertheless, it is a fact that thousands if not millions of people watched the reunion and we would not have expected less from a TV show that is clearly part of pop culture and an iconic program for masses.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
A SMOKING GUN
Something that is obvious; an indisputable truth.
You should have seen the smoking gun; that man could not be trusted.
HIDDEN AGENDA
Something that may refer to a secret plan or an implication.
I would not have expected Freddy to have a hidden agenda.
A SHOT IN THE DARK
To have an ide or suspicion about someone or something.
Thank God I had already gotten a shot in the dark about Tim, he almost got away with that.
NUTS AND BOLTS
The detailed information about someone or something and how it works.
If it had been me, I would have gone nut and bolts with Jenny; now she’s gone!
AN INSIDE STORY
Considered as an advice or a hot tip.
What an inside story John has just dropped us.
A STRAW IN THE WIND
It refers to an indication or sign that one can see or get from someone or something.
We should have seen the straw in the wind; now, we can’t do anything.
UPPER HAND
It means someone or something has a position of advantage and control.
Fortunately, I had already upper-handed the rest of the contestants.
TIP OF THE ICEBERG
The small piece or amount of something that we can see.
Handing over the project was just the tip of the iceberg.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We are able to express opinions, suggestions and expectations in the past by using the following structures. Check the chart.
STRUCTURES
STATEMENTS
QUESTIONS
Should  Have + Past Participle
Dylan should have called them before going.
What should he have done before going?
If it had been me, I should have brought more money.
What should you have done?
Would  have + Past Participle
My family would have wanted him to be different, but he wasn’t.
How would have your family wanted him to be?
He would not have expected me to drop school.
would he have expected you to drop school?
Must have + Past Participle
We must have seen the straw in the wind, but we did not.
Would you have seen the straw in the wind?
If he had done things differently, the boss would have given him the chance.
What if he had done things differently?
slideDifferences.publishedText: We are able to express opinions, suggestions and expectations in the past by using the following structures. Check the chart. STRUCTURES STATEMENTS QUESTIONS Should Have + Past Participle Dylan should have called them before going. What should he have done before going? If it had been me, I should have brought more money. What should you have done? Would have + Past Participle My family would have wanted him to be different, but he wasn’t. How would have your family wanted him to be? He would not have expected me to drop school. Would he have expected you to drop school? Must have + Past Participle We must have seen the straw in the wind, but we did not. Would you have seen the straw in the wind? If he had not done things that way , the boss must have given him the chance. What if he had not done things that way?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
To Consider

This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional. 
Modals + Have + past participle are still the base of the structure.
We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 
The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 
All of them state a hypothetical or unreal situation in the past.

All of them state a hypothetical or unreal situation in the past.

This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional.

We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 
The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 
All of them state a hypothetical or unreal situation in the past, EXCEPT -regret + V(ing) - that can be used in different tenses logically.

texts: C. Read the following article  and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. You can read the full version on the link provided for further activities.
Regret can Seriously Damage your Mental Health

here was once a banker in his 50s who had worked seven days a week for 25 years and become a very wealthy man. Then, at the apex of his career, he looked around him and realised that he had entirely neglected his family; as a result, his family had rejected him. The regret was overwhelming, and came out in panic attacks every Sunday. Would this man be able to find a way out of this cruel place he had created for himself?

This man was a patient of the psychoanalyst David Morgan, of the Institute of Psychoanalysis, who spent several years helping him explore what had compelled him to work so hard and to ignore his children (he has been anonymised and gave Morgan permission to use his case). It became clear that this need to become richer than everyone else had roots in his very early childhood, when he watched his parents nearly starve to death during the 1980s miners’ strike. He had, unconsciously, repeated this by impoverishing his children by not being there for them, in turn impoverishing himself of these loving relationships, in his efforts to overcome the traumatic poverty of his childhood.

“That complicated understanding,” Morgan explains, “freed things up, setting his regret in a generational context so he didn’t have to feel quite so guilty for acting something out, because it was beyond his ken. It doesn’t mean that he can’t feel real pain, but that pain is given a sense of history.” This meant his regret could be understood and given meaning – and that changed his life.

texts: Regret can be all-consuming, and it can destroy lives. We can see it all around us, whether it is the man who cannot forgive himself for cheating on his first girlfriend and has not had a serious relationship in 30 years. Or the woman who is so tied up in wishing she’d had a child with her ex-partner, instead of breaking up with him, that she cannot find happiness in her current circumstances.

It is not unusual for patients to seek therapy because they feel plagued by regret and unable to live full lives because of it, says Morgan, whether it is over affairs, career choices or relationships. The kind of regret that brings people to his consulting room is “paranoid and persecutory. It’s: ‘Oh God, I’m so terrible, I’m dreadful,’” he says. It is self-flagellation, and it can be incredibly damaging to our mental health. It is exhausting, it sucks all joy and fulfilment from our days and it leaves us stuck, always looking backwards and unable to move forward in our lives.

The cognitive behaviour therapist Windy Dryden says that, when we are trapped in this cycle of regret, characterised by rigidity and inflexibility, we only seem able to blame ourselves for what has happened, rather than seeing our behaviour in a wider context and understanding why we took the path we did based on the information we had at the time. Under these conditions, regret will become toxic.

STATEMENTS
QUESTIONS
Should  Have + Past Participle
I  should have told them the truth before,

What should you have said?

would you really have expected nothing from them?

To Consider

This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional. 
Should + Have + past participle is still used here.
We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 
The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 
All of them state a hypothetical or unreal situation in the past, EXCEPT -regret + V(ing) - that can be used in different tenses logically.

C. Read the following article  and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. You can read the full version on the link provided for further activities.
Regret can Seriously Damage your Mental Health

here was once a banker in his 50s who had worked seven days a week for 25 years and become a very wealthy man. Then, at the apex of his career, he looked around him and realised that he had entirely neglected his family; as a result, his family had rejected him. The regret was overwhelming, and came out in panic attacks every Sunday. Would this man be able to find a way out of this cruel place he had created for himself?

This man was a patient of the psychoanalyst David Morgan, of the Institute of Psychoanalysis, who spent several years helping him explore what had compelled him to work so hard and to ignore his children (he has been anonymised and gave Morgan permission to use his case). It became clear that this need to become richer than everyone else had roots in his very early childhood, when he watched his parents nearly starve to death during the 1980s miners’ strike. He had, unconsciously, repeated this by impoverishing his children by not being there for them, in turn impoverishing himself of these loving relationships, in his efforts to overcome the traumatic poverty of his childhood.

“That complicated understanding,” Morgan explains, “freed things up, setting his regret in a generational context so he didn’t have to feel quite so guilty for acting something out, because it was beyond his ken. It doesn’t mean that he can’t feel real pain, but that pain is given a sense of history.” This meant his regret could be understood and given meaning – and that changed his life.

To Consider

This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional. 
Could / May / Might work with Have + Past Participle.
We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 
The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 
All of them state possible events in the past. 
The probability is higher depending on the modal we use as we learned before.

texts: C. Read the following article  and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. You can read the full version on the link provided for further activities.

Around 66 million years ago, a 14 km-wide asteroid smashed into our planet. An estimated 15 billion tonnes of soot spread through the atmosphere, creating one long night that lasted several years and made photosynthesis all but impossible. It heralded an endless winter that saw average temperatures fall by as much as 28oC. These are the conditions that the few wretched creatures that survived the initial impact had to endure – not to mention the earthquakes, tsunamis, wildfires and volcanic eruptions that swiftly followed in its wake.

Around three-quarters of all species went extinct and no animal bigger than a Labrador dog survived. But according to researchers at the University of Texas, things could have been very different. They reported findings that had the asteroid struck Earth just a few minutes earlier, it would have hit the deep ocean rather than the shallow sea of the Yucatan Peninsula in present-day Mexico.

Had that been the case, then the damage would have been more localised. Some of the dinosaurs far from the impact site might have survived, and the world would be a different place today. In our own history, only the feathered theropod dinosaurs (a group of bipedal dinosaurs) we know as birds made it through the calamity, but how would things have turned out if their larger relatives had joined them? Would dinosaurs still be alive today and could mammals such as humans have evolved? What would our world look like if we shared it with the descendants of animals like T. rex and Triceratops?

texts: “I’m sure a fairly nice diversity of non-avian dinosaurs would still be here,” says Dr Stephen Brusatte, a palaeontology at the University of Edinburgh. “If there was no sudden, catastrophic shock of the asteroid, I really don’t see anything that’s happened since – whether it was the spread of grasslands; changing ocean currents; the separation of Antarctica from South America, which caused a cold snap; or the more recent Ice Ages – that would have knocked off the dinosaurs.”

Over the years many have tried to imagine what kind of creatures dinosaurs might have evolved into had they survived. The most famous attempt is a 1988 book called The New Dinosaurs: An Alternative Evolution, by Scottish geologist and author Dougal Dixon. For this magnificent work of speculative zoology, Dixon conjured up creatures such as the ‘cutlasstooth’ – a pack-hunting, sabre-toothed predator from South America; the ‘cribrum’ – a flamingo-like, filter-feeding theropod from Australia; and the ‘gourmand’ – a relative of T. rex that lost its front limbs entirely and developed a distensible jaw to allow it to rapidly swallow prey whole, much like a snake.

Perhaps this last idea isn’t entirely wide of the mark. Dr Tom Holtz, an expert on theropod dinosaurs at the University of Maryland in the US, says that both tyrannosaurs and abelisaurs, the two types of big meat-eater present in the Late Cretaceous, are notable for their tiny forelimbs. “Given that arms were non-critical for hunting, it’s possible that a Cenozoic [current geological era] tyrannosaur could have been armless,” says Holtz.

PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
WHEN PIGS FLY
To be sure something will never happen
You’ll get that once pigs fly.
ONCE IN A BLUE MOON
A very rare event to happen.
John gets straight As once in a blue moon.
HELL FREEZES
Something impossible to occur.
They could have gotten the offer if hell had frozen.
FEW AND FAR BETWEEN
To indicate rarely seen events.
Just in a few and far between, he might have obtained the score.
NOT TO HOLD SOMEONE’S BREATH
Expresses something people hope for will likely never happen.
He should not have held his breath on that.
TO GET BLOOD FROM A STONE
Generally taken to mean a pointless task due to its difficulty.
Don’t you try get blood from that stone; she will never like you.
TWELFTH OF NEVER
Something that will happen on the "Twelfth of Never" will never come to pass.
She could have answered yes in the twelfth of never.
TIBB’S EVE
To refer to something that does not / did not / will not exist.
We’re coming back on Tibb’s eve.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

We are able to express opinions, suggestions and expectations in the past by using the following structures. Check the chart.
STRUCTURES
STATEMENTS
QUESTIONS
Could + Have + Past Participle
I  could have gotten lost if we had not seen then on time.
What could have happened to them?
You could have said that before all went to nothing.
What could I  have said?
May + Have + Past Participle
John may have caught that flu at the hospital.
Where may John  have caught that flu?
We may have called a few times; but he never picked up.
would you really have expected nothing from them?
Might + Have + Past Participle
I  might have eaten a cheese burger once.
Did you eat a burger even being a vegetarian?
They might have been here but they are gone now.
Were they here before?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
To Consider

This structures do not necessarily work using the third conditional. 
Could / May / Might work with Have + Past Participle.
We can use yes/no questions or Wh-words to go interrogative. 
The context or the joining statements attached to these grammar structures are important and they need to be cohesive and logical. 
All of them state possible events in the past. 
The probability is higher depending on the modal we use as we learned before.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We can use these structures to state the following functions:
Functions
Examples
1
Express Probabilities in the past.
They  might  have ended up  together but Shane ruined it.
2
Make guesses about past events.
They could have gotten lost the way since they did not arrive last night.
3.
State impossible past events.
If Kyle was at work, he could have not committed the murder
To consider 
We can use all of possibility modals for functions 1 and 2. 
Function 2 needs a logic complement to make it look like a guess not as a possibility. 
Function number three works with Could + Have only. 
You may see function 3 also working with CAN’T + Have.

C. Read the following article  and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. You can read the full version on the link provided for further activities.
What if Dinosaurs had survived?

Around 66 million years ago, a 14 km-wide asteroid smashed into our planet. An estimated 15 billion tonnes of soot spread through the atmosphere, creating one long night that lasted several years and made photosynthesis all but impossible. It heralded an endless winter that saw average temperatures fall by as much as 28oC. These are the conditions that the few wretched creatures that survived the initial impact had to endure – not to mention the earthquakes, tsunamis, wildfires and volcanic eruptions that swiftly followed in its wake.

Around three-quarters of all species went extinct and no animal bigger than a Labrador dog survived. But according to researchers at the University of Texas, things could have been very different. They reported findings that had the asteroid struck Earth just a few minutes earlier, it would have hit the deep ocean rather than the shallow sea of the Yucatan Peninsula in present-day Mexico.

Had that been the case, then the damage would have been more localised. Some of the dinosaurs far from the impact site might have survived, and the world would be a different place today. In our own history, only the feathered theropod dinosaurs (a group of bipedal dinosaurs) we know as birds made it through the calamity, but how would things have turned out if their larger relatives had joined them? Would dinosaurs still be alive today and could mammals such as humans have evolved? What would our world look like if we shared it with the descendants of animals like T. rex and Triceratops?

texts: We are able to express ideas about things or event likely to happen through the use of different expressions and regular grammar.
John, we should call Tim, what if he takes a stab at the meeting and all goes wrong?
Imagine if Mary shows up at the wedding, we need to warn them.
We should phone them in case they are lost; don’t you think?
Delia is talking to Jim in advance, supposing that he wants to come and make a scene

To Consider

We work with these phrases using the simple present tense. 
When using -what if- we have to close the sentence with a question mark. 
The context will determine if the situation likely to happen is in the present or future. 
Modals can help out build a context.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
Possible Potential Outcomes from COVID-19 Complications on Testes: Lesson from SARS Infection

Coronavirus infection disease-2019 (COVID-19) gained worldwide fame after deadly outbreak in China and its subsequent spread to many countries. So far, COVID-19 is not fully contained, and new cases are arising on daily bases in various countries, Imagine if it keeps growing. Due to zoonotic nature and human-to-human spread, COVID-19 is considered pandemic with more causalities in developing countries. Full genome analysis revealed its resemblance with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) virus with minor variation in non-structural proteins. Both viruses use the common angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE2) receptor to attach to the epithelial cells of the target organs. Currently, in case someone gets COVID-19, those patients are treated with drugs that are used for lungs infections. However, ACE2 has high expression in other human organs such as kidney and testes. So what if that’s not enough? Thus, it is assumed that, like SARS, it may have adverse effects on other vital organs, which have dominant expression of ACE2. In testis, SARS affected patients displayed peritubular fibrosis, extensive germ cell disruption, damage of blood-testis barrier integrity and more frequent occurrence of apoptosis. Here, we critically discuss the possible adverse effects of COVID-19 on the testes of patients along with future precautions to overcome the complications of reproductive organs.

PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
HAZARD A GUESS
To have a guess about someone or something.
He always hazards guesses, so be careful.
GRASP AT A STRAW
To be unsure about something and still state an opinion.
I think he is just grasping at a straw.
READ SOMEONE’S MIND
To deduce what someone else is thinking.
She will never call; It’s like I read her mind.
A SHOT IN THE DARK
To venture guessing something you are not certain about.
John accused Oliver, he just took a shot in the dark.
ANYONE’S GUESS
A mystery or something unpredictable.
It's anyone's guess what his next book will be about.
TAKE A STAB AT
To give it a try or a shot.
Mary went for it and took a stab at the application.
SEAT-OF-THE-PANTS
To describe something improvised or done based on prior experience.
Why are you doing this by seat-of-the-pants?
BARK UP THE WRONG TREE
To be wrong about something or someone; To be wrong about the reasons or ways to achieve something.
Stop accusing me lady, you’re barking up the wrong tree,
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
Possible Potential Outcomes from COVID-19 Complications on Testes: Lesson from SARS Infection

Coronavirus infection disease-2019 (COVID-19) gained worldwide fame after deadly outbreak in China and its subsequent spread to many countries. So far, COVID-19 is not fully contained, and new cases are arising on daily bases in various countries, Imagine if it keeps growing. Due to zoonotic nature and human-to-human spread, COVID-19 is considered pandemic with more causalities in developing countries. Full genome analysis revealed its resemblance with severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) virus with minor variation in non-structural proteins. Both viruses use the common angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE2) receptor to attach to the epithelial cells of the target organs. Currently, in case someone gets COVID-19, those patients are treated with drugs that are used for lungs infections. However, ACE2 has high expression in other human organs such as kidney and testes. So what if that’s not enough? Thus, it is assumed that, like SARS, it may have adverse effects on other vital organs, which have dominant expression of ACE2. In testis, SARS affected patients displayed peritubular fibrosis, extensive germ cell disruption, damage of blood-testis barrier integrity and more frequent occurrence of apoptosis. Here, we critically discuss the possible adverse effects of COVID-19 on the testes of patients along with future precautions to overcome the complications of reproductive organs.
                                                                                             

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       Adapted from: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33115584/

Language bricks

texts: We are able to express ideas about things or event not likely to happen through the use of different expressions and regular grammar.
What if Jane came tonight to the party? Just picture how awkward it would be.
Imagine you fell in front of your classmates; would you laugh at yourself?
If only you could come home these days. / If only I had more time, but I am always busy.
I wish we didn’t feel the pinch but there’s nothing we could do. / I wish it could be different.

To Consider

We work with these phrases using the simple past tense. 
When using -what if- we have to close the sentence with a question mark. 
Could and would play a major role.

texts: We can use the grammar presented to talk about the following function:
Express ideas or events not likely to be true or to happen.

What if Jill had money? Would you guys accept her in the club?

Imagine they won the competition; they would never stop talking about it.

If only she  saw the fit of the project, she could be more supportive.

I wish he came to me first so I could help him.
There are contexts where -could- and -would- express wishes for the future. E.G I don’t like my job; I wish I could get a new one.
That sound is so annoying; I wish it would stop.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. Check the full article in the link below.
Achieving Your Wishes : Will Wishing Work?

Do you wish you had a better job, bigger house, more friends, better health, less worries, and greater happiness? We all engage in wishing, but should we? Should we wish for more or be satisfied with what we have? Why can't we do both? Just because we are satisfied with what we have doesn't mean we can't or shouldn't wish for more. After all, isn't self-improvement or personal-development about wishing for more?

No, there isn't anything wrong with wishing. A wish is merely the voice of our Higher Self reminding us that we have boundless potential and urging us to take advantage of it. If anything, we should wish to have, be, and do more because that's how we help to create a better world; if only we always thought that way.. It is only when we have more than we need that we can share what we have with those who have less than they need. It is only when we are healthy that we can help the sick. And it is only when we are strong that we can help the weak. As you can see, wishing plays an important role, for we either allow ourselves to become what others will make of us, or we wish to become something better.

Did you ever toss a coin into a wishing well and make a wish? What if you had your own wishing well? Aware of it or not, that's precisely what we have. We have a personal genie within us. It is our subconscious. Its sole purpose is to serve us. It serves us by regulating our heart and breathing rate, body temperature, and the flow of hormones, just to name a few of its many functions. But another major function of the subconscious is to grant our every wish! And it works tirelessly, 24/7, granting us what it believes we want.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
FILL THE PINCH
To experience hardship, especially financial.
Staff, we’re beginning to feel the pinch as the dispute entered its third week.
SEE THE FIT
To consider it correct or acceptable to do something.
why did the company see fit to give you the job?
KNOCK ON WOOD
said after a confident or positive statement, to express a hope for one's good luck to continue.
I haven't been banned yet, knock on wood.
FIRE IN THE BELLY
A powerful sense of ambition or determination.
He lacks the fire in his belly necessary to seek the presidency.
HOPE AGAINST HOPE
Hope or wish for with little reason or justification.
I'm hoping against hope that someone will return my wallet.
FOOL’S PARADISE
A state of happiness based on a person's not knowing about or denying the existence of potential trouble.
They were living in a fool's paradise, refusing to accept that they were in debt.
BRASS RING
A very desirable prize, goal, or opportunity
He made his first try for the brass ring when he ran for mayor a few years ago.
GAME PLAN
A strategy worked out in advance, especially in sports, politics, or business.
If he has a game plan for winning the deal, only he understands it.
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We are able to express ideas about things or event not likely to happen through the use of different expressions and regular grammar.
PHRASES
EXAMPLES
What if…
What if Jane came tonight to the party? Just picture how awkward it would be.
Imagine that / if…
Imagine you fell in front of your classmates; would you laugh at yourself?
If only…
If only you could come home these days. / If only I had more time, but I am always busy.
I wish…
I wish we didn’t feel the pinch but there’s nothing we could do. / I wish it could be different.
To Consider

We work with these phrases using the simple past tense. 
When using -what if- we have to close the sentence with a question mark. 
Could and would play a major role.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We can use the grammar presented to talk about the following function:
Functions
Examples
1
Express ideas or events not likely to be true or to happen.
What if Jill had money? Would you guys accept her in the club?

Imagine they won the competition; they would never stop talking about it.

If only she  saw the fit of the project, she could be more supportive.

I wish he came to me first so I could help him.
To consider 
There are contexts where -could- and -would- express wishes for the future. E.G I don’t like my job; I wish I could get a new one.
                   That sound is so annoying; I wish it would stop.

texts: We are able to express ideas about things or event that did not happened through the use of different expressions and regular grammar.
What if Charles had taken  Mary to the party? Hell would have loosened there!
Imagine you hadn’t called  Joe’s parents; When would they have known?
Supposing we had not gone to the doctor, we could have gotten worse.
I wish I had called her; Now, I will never know if she felt the same for me.

To Consider

We work with these phrases using the past perfect tense.
When using -what if- we have to close the sentence with a question mark. 
Could and would play a major role. Especially for complementing the sentences. 
Some other modals may be useful depending on the context.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. Check the full article in the link below.
Global Disasters that never Came to happen: The Impending Ice Age

An April 28, 1975 article in Newsweek Magazine titled "The Cooling World" warned that the world could freeze over before we knew it. A year earlier, Time ran an article titled, "A New Ice Age?" The media of the mid-70's latched onto the idea of impending icy death, imagine if it had become true. But where did this come from? Between 1945 and the 1970's global temperatures had decreased. Scientists have since figured out that sulphate aerosols caused cooling, by blocking and reflecting sunlight as well as serving as seeds for cloud coverage. At the same time scientific papers explaining about how the earth's orbital patterns affect global weather and the creation of ice ages were being published. The media seemed to pick up geologist saying an ice age could be soon — but not really understanding that thousands of years is "soon" to a geologist; but what if that had happened? We would not probable have written this article.

Despite the media hype, the scientific journals were either unsure about how humans were affecting the climate, or already predicting the possibility of global warming due to CO2. Current research shows the high level of CO2 in the atmosphere is preventing any growth of the ice sheets. The Ice Age fear has come back recently, most likely because of the 2012 hysteria, but this time in conjunction with the sun's solar cycles. Bad Astronomy explains why you don't need invest in parkas quite yet. Incidentally, Newsweek issued a correction to the 1975 article in 2006, since by then it was clear an Ice Age hadn't wiped us all out. If only people had been more cautious in the information they linked, we (new generations) may have turned more eager for facts than farandula.

PHRASES
MEANING
EXAMPLE
CASTLES IN THE AIR
To have big dreams about an idea or project that may not come true.
What if all this had been just castles in the air?
CLASS ACT
A person or thing displaying impressive and stylish excellence.
the writing and the look of the magazine make it a real class act.
HUNKY DORY
Expression used to say all is going well.
Everything is hunky-dory.
QUEER AS A THREE-DOLLAR BILL
Completely and obviously false or fake; not genuine or authentic in the slightest..
The guy claims to teach you how to get rich in a hurry, but the whole thing sounds as queer as a three-dollar bill.
LARGER THAN LIFE
To attract special attention because of unusual and flamboyant appearance or behavior or seem disproportionately important.
your problems seem larger than life at that time of night.
OFF THE MARK
When something or someone is incorrect or inaccurate.
The accusation was a little wide of the mark.
OFF BASE
To be mistaken.
Your argument is so off base.
OFF THE WALL
To be eccentric or unconventional. Some other times to be really angry.
The president was off the wall about the article.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We are able to express ideas about things or event that did not happened through the use of different expressions and regular grammar.
PHRASES
EXAMPLES
What if…
What if Charles had taken  Mary to the party? Hell would have loosened there!
Imagine that / if…
Imagine you hadn’t called  Joe’s parents; When would they have known?
Suppose / Supposing that
Supposing we had not gone to the doctor, we could have gotten worse.
I wish…
I wish I had called her; Now, I will never know if she felt the same for me.
To Consider

We work with these phrases using the past perfect tense.
When using -what if- we have to close the sentence with a question mark. 
Could and would play a major role. Especially for complementing the sentences. 
Some other modals may be useful depending on the context.

C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. Check the full article in the link below.
Global Disasters that never Came to happen: The Impending Ice Age

An April 28, 1975 article in Newsweek Magazine titled "The Cooling World" warned that the world could freeze over before we knew it. A year earlier, Time ran an article titled, "A New Ice Age?" The media of the mid-70's latched onto the idea of impending icy death, imagine if it had become true. But where did this come from? Between 1945 and the 1970's global temperatures had decreased. Scientists have since figured out that sulphate aerosols caused cooling, by blocking and reflecting sunlight as well as serving as seeds for cloud coverage. At the same time scientific papers explaining about how the earth's orbital patterns affect global weather and the creation of ice ages were being published. The media seemed to pick up geologist saying an ice age could be soon — but not really understanding that thousands of years is "soon" to a geologist; but what if that had happened? We would not probable have written this article.

 Despite the media hype, the scientific journals were either unsure about how humans were affecting the climate, or already predicting the possibility of global warming due to CO2. Current research shows the high level of CO2 in the atmosphere is preventing any growth of the ice sheets. The Ice Age fear has come back recently, most likely because of the 2012 hysteria, but this time in conjunction with the sun's solar cycles. Bad Astronomy explains why you don't need invest in parkas quite yet. Incidentally, Newsweek issued a correction to the 1975 article in 2006, since by then it was clear an Ice Age hadn't wiped us all out. If only people had been more cautious in the information they linked, we (new generations) may have turned more eager for facts than farandula.

In the long term, over a long period of time.

-I should call Annie,

texts: We are able to express ideas about things or events yet to happen through two main grammar structures.

The guests are coming at 8PM. I’ll have finished cooking by then.

In two years’ time, I’ll have had my kids, so I’ll be a parent. 

Will the kids have gone to bed when I get back?

When you get out of the office tomorrow, I’ll be boarding a plane.

Come on July, I won’t be working then. 

Will you be starting work earlier with your new job?

To Consider

Future perfect works with Will + Have + Past participle. 
It uses time phrases like: By then, In some years’ time, when clauses, by the time  etc. 
Future continuous works with To be + V(ing). 
The time phrases for future continuous may be shared with future perfect; though, the ones used here are more specific as seen in the examples. 
Both can add -Wh words- to make questions.

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and have a discussion with the teacher. After that, read aloud the text to your teacher. Check the full article in the link below.
The expert guide to space colonies

With our rising planet’s population competing for space and resources, some people are convinced we need to look beyond Earth to help ensure humanity’s survival; What will we have had when that time comes?. As Elon Musk, the entrepreneur behind space tourism company SpaceX put it recently: “I think there is a strong argument for making life multi-planetary in order to safeguard the existence of humanity in the event that something catastrophic were to happen.”

Even if you don’t believe this bleak vision, it’s hard to ignore the eternal human instinct to discover the undiscovered – an urge that could push people beyond the safety of our planet, and we reckon we will be doing something about it when time comes. And there might not be as many hurdles as you might think. “We are at the level of technology where we can imagine leaving the planet for a few nearby places in our Solar System,” former astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman, who will present his ideas at our summit, told BBC Future previously. “The Moon is just around the corner, and Mars isn’t that far away. We have the possibility of at least making the first steps of those voyages in our own lifetimes.”
What could a space colony look like?

One possible idea goes as far back as the 1920s. Austro-Hungarian rocket pioneer Herman Potočnik imagined a circular spacecraft  - rather like a flying saucer – that rotates to create artificial gravity while a large, concave mirror could focus sunlight for an energy source.  As far-fetched as this may sound, the idea has lingered over the years – most notably in the mid-1970s by the late Princeton physicist Gerard O’Neill, and again by the space think tank British Interplanetary Society. Before you dismiss the idea of floating colonies completely, it’s worth noting that the British Interplanetary Society predicted we would reach the Moon three decades before it actually happened, so imagine where it will have gotten once it sets its mind on it.

The expert guide to space colonies With our rising planet’s population competing for space and resources, some people are convinced we need to look beyond Earth to help ensure humanity’s survival; What will we have had when that time comes?. As Elon Musk, the entrepreneur behind space tourism company SpaceX put it recently: “I think there is a strong argument for making life multiplanetary in order to safeguard the existence of humanity in the event that something catastrophic were to happen.” Even if you don’t believe this bleak vision, it’s hard to ignore the eternal human instinct to discover the undiscovered – an urge that could push people beyond the safety of our planet, and we reckon we will be doing something about it when time comes. And there might not be as many hurdles as you might think. “We are at the level of technology where we can imagine leaving the planet for a few nearby places in our Solar System,” former astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman, who will present his ideas at our summit, told BBC Future previously. “The Moon is just around the corner, and Mars isn’t that far away. We have the possibility of at least making the first steps of those voyages in our own lifetimes.” What could a space colony look like? One possible idea goes as far back as the 1920s. Austro-Hungarian rocket pioneer Herman Potočnik imagined a circular spacecraft - rather like a flying saucer – that rotates to create artificial gravity while a large, concave mirror could focus sunlight for an energy source. As far-fetched as this may sound, the idea has lingered over the years – most notably in the mid-1970s by the late Princeton physicist Gerard O’Neill, and again by the space think tank British Interplanetary Society. Before you dismiss the idea of floating colonies completely, it’s worth noting that the British Interplanetary Society predicted we would reach the Moon three decades before it actually happened, so imagine where it will have gotten once it sets its mind on it.
